review.detail: The left-continuous and right-continuous generalized inverses can differ at flat pieces; the cited source fixes the right-continuous convention. Villani's Theorem 2.18 gives product-cost maximization for bounded marginals through $|a-b|^2=a^2+b^2-2ab$. Reflecting one marginal gives countermonotonic minimization. Truncating the unbounded marginal and passing to the limit is justified by the bounded other marginal and the stated finite first moment. Thus the supplied source supports both formulas and attainments without requiring a second moment.

\label{thm:1d_ot}
    Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on $\mathbb{R}$ with quantile functions $Q_\mu$ and $Q_\nu$.
Suppose either that $\mu$ has bounded support and $\nu$ has a finite first moment, or vice versa,
and let the cost be the simple product $c(a,b) = a \cdot b$.
Then, the minimum and maximum of the expected cost over all valid couplings are completely characterized by the countermonotonic and comonotonic couplings, respectively:

\begin{align*}
        \min_{\pi \in \Pi(\mu, \nu)} \int_{\mathbb{R}^2} a \cdot b \, \mathrm{d}\pi(a, b) &= \int_0^1 Q_\mu(t) Q_\nu(1-t) \, \mathrm{d}t, \\

\max_{\pi \in \Pi(\mu, \nu)} \int_{\mathbb{R}^2} a \cdot b \, \mathrm{d}\pi(a, b) &= \int_0^1 Q_\mu(t) Q_\nu(t) \, \mathrm{d}t.

The minimum is attained by the countermonotonic coupling $(Q_\mu(\xi), Q_\nu(1-\xi))$,
and the maximum by the comonotonic coupling $(Q_\mu(\xi), Q_\nu(\xi))$,

PROVENANCE
==========
Cited work: Cedric Villani, "Topics in Optimal Transportation", Graduate Studies in Mathematics
  vol. 58, American Mathematical Society. The citing paper's bibliography gives the 2021 reprint
  (doi 10.1090/gsm/058).
Version read: a scan of the printed book (382 PDF pages, no text layer), supplied by the paper's
  owner as the URL https://www.math.ucla.edu/~wgangbo/Cedric-Villani.pdf (fetched 2026-10-11;
  sha256 8db5bff147e12ba4abfb7c917f41558a391ef42849789435ce15b43d094889ea, 24,312,654 bytes). The scan shows no edition statement on the pages read; the reprint is
  not known to differ in this section, but that was not checked.
Locator: Chapter 2 "Geometry of Optimal Transportation", Section 2.2 "The real line",
  subsections 2.2.1-2.2.2, printed pages 73-75 (PDF pages 87-89 of the scan). The citing paper
  gives no theorem number; this is the one-dimensional optimal transportation theorem of the
  book.
How the text was obtained: the three pages were rendered to PNG (130 dpi) and READ BY EYE, then
  typed. No OCR. Mathematics is typed in LaTeX-like notation; the typing conventions are the
  fetcher's, the content is the page's. The three page images are kept beside this file as
  villani2021topics.source.p73.png, .p74.png, .p75.png.

DEFINITIONS (printed p. 73, subsection "2.2.1. Cumulative distribution functions")
=================================================================================
  Any probability measure \mu on R can be represented by its distribution function, or, in a
  less ambiguous terminology, its cumulative distribution function:

      F(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} d\mu = \mu[(-\infty, x]].

  Recall from elementary probability theory that F is right-continuous, nondecreasing, and
  F(-\infty) = 0, F(+\infty) = 1.
  Then, one can define the generalized inverse of F on [0,1] by

      F^{-1}(t) = \inf { x \in R ; F(x) > t }.

(printed p. 74)
  The generalized inverse of F is also right-continuous (see Figure 2.5). Note the inequalities

      \forall x \in R,  F^{-1}(F(x)) \geq x ;      \forall t \in [0,1],  F(F^{-1}(t)) \geq t.

  As for probability measures on the product space R x R, they can be represented by joint
  two-dimensional cumulative distribution functions:

      H(x_0, y_0) = \int_{R(x_0,y_0)} d\pi = \pi[R(x_0, y_0)],

  where R(x_0, y_0) is the rectangle made of all points (x,y) \in R^2 with x \leq x_0,
  y \leq y_0. We will use the notation d\pi = dH. A function H on R^2 which is nondecreasing,
  right-continuous in both variables x and y, and has limits 0 and 1 at (-\infty,-\infty) and
  (+\infty,+\infty) respectively, gives rise to a unique probability measure on R^2. [...]

THE RESULT (printed pp. 74-75, subsection "2.2.2. Optimal transportation theorem on the line")
=============================================================================================
  We can now state the solution to the optimal transportation problem in terms of cumulative
  distribution functions. The following theorem was already known to Hoeffding and Frechet.

  Theorem 2.18 (Optimal transportation theorem for a quadratic cost on R). Let \mu, \nu be two
  probability measures on R, with respective cumulative distribution functions F and G. Let
  \pi be the probability measure on R^2 with joint two-dimensional cumulative distribution
  function

      (2.46)   H(x,y) = \min( F(x), G(y) ).

  Then, \pi belongs to \Pi(\mu,\nu), and is optimal in the Kantorovich transportation problem
  between \mu and \nu for the quadratic cost function c(x,y) = |x - y|^2. Moreover, the value
  of the optimal transportation cost is

      (2.47)   T_2(\mu,\nu) = \int_0^1 | F^{-1}(t) - G^{-1}(t) |^2 dt.

  Remarks 2.19. (i) The Hoeffding-Frechet theorem states that a nonnegative function H on
  R^2, nondecreasing and right-continuous in each argument, defines a probability measure \pi
  on R^2 with given marginals \mu, \nu if and only if

      \forall (x,y) \in R^2,    F(x) + G(y) - 1 \leq H(x,y) \leq \min[ F(x), G(y) ],

  where F and G are the cumulative distribution functions associated with \mu and \nu
  respectively. For background on this theorem, see for instance [211].

  (ii) In fact, the \pi constructed in Theorem 2.18 is optimal whatever the convex cost. More
  precisely, \pi is optimal as soon as the cost function c(x,y) takes the form c(x - y), where
  c is a convex nonnegative symmetric function on R. In this case the optimal transportation
  cost is

      T_c(\mu,\nu) = \int_0^1 c( F^{-1}(t) - G^{-1}(t) ) dt.

  In the case of a concave cost function, the situation is completely different: see the
  explanations and references at the end of this chapter.

  (iii) In particular, the total transportation cost associated with the cost function
  c(x,y) = |x - y| is

      (2.48)   T_1(\mu,\nu) = \int_0^1 | F^{-1}(t) - G^{-1}(t) | dt = \int_R | F(x) - G(x) | dx,

  where the second inequality [sic: printed "inequality"] is a consequence of Fubini's theorem
  (exercise!). Thus, in this case, the optimal transportation cost coincides with the L^1
  distance between cumulative distribution functions.

  (iv) If \mu does not give mass to points, then T = G^{-1} o F transports \mu onto \nu, and

      (2.49)   \int_{-\infty}^{x} d\mu = \int_{-\infty}^{T(x)} d\nu.

  This expresses the general fact that the solution to the transportation problem is given by
  the monotone rearrangement of \mu onto \nu [...]

NOTE BY THE FETCHER (not part of the cited work)
================================================
1. What the source states: optimality of the comonotone coupling (joint CDF min(F,G)) for the
   QUADRATIC cost |x-y|^2, and by Remark 2.19(ii) for costs c(x-y) with c convex, nonnegative
   and symmetric; the optimal value as an integral of quantile functions. The standing
   framework of the book's Kantorovich problem (finiteness of the cost, moment conditions) is
   set in its Chapters 1-2 and was not copied here.
2. What the source does NOT state on these pages: a result for the product cost c(a,b) = a*b;
   the minimum of \int a*b d\pi (the countermonotone coupling); the moment condition "one
   measure has bounded support and the other a finite first moment". The lower bound
   F(x)+G(y)-1 of Remark 2.19(i) is the CDF of the countermonotone coupling, but the source
   draws no optimality conclusion from it here.
3. Generalized inverse: the source uses F^{-1}(t) = inf{x : F(x) > t} (strict inequality, the
   right-continuous version). The citing paper writes "quantile functions Q_\mu".
4. The second cited work, Galichon (2016), Optimal Transport Methods in Economics, was not
   obtained.

\label{prop:sharpness}
    Suppose the observed distribution $\mathbb{P}_{obs}$ is generated by a true structural model satisfying \cref{asp:structure}.

Let $\tilde{\pi}$ be any probability measure on $\mathcal{Y} \times \mathcal{Y} \times [0,1] \times \mathcal{X}$ whose $(Y(w), U, X)$-marginals $\tilde{\pi}_w$ satisfy $(\tilde{\pi}_0, \tilde{\pi}_1) \in \Gamma(\mathbb{P}_{obs})$.
Then there exists a joint distribution of the latent and observable variables $(Y(0), Y(1), U, X, Z, W)$ such that:

(ii)] \cref{asp:structure} holds for $(Y(0), Y(1), U, X, Z, W)$;
        \item[

(iii)] the induced distribution of $(Z, X, W, Y)$ exactly matches $\mathbb{P}_{obs}$.
    \end{enumerate}

Conversely, every joint marginal $\tilde{\pi}$ arising from a distribution of $(Y(0), Y(1), U, X, Z, W)$ satisfying \textup{(ii)}--\textup{(iii)} has $(Y(w), U, X)$-marginals in $\Gamma(\mathbb{P}_{obs})$ for $w \in \{0, 1\}$.

Pointwise endpoint assignments give both tail bounds, and the graded sharpness result supplies observational compatibility. The deferred proof is explicitly identified immediately after the theorem. The inherited quantile convention and owner reading settle quantiles and conditioning; an attained zero propensity adds only a zero restriction, and $p_K=1$ gives a zero tail.

review.detail: The core faithfully carries the structural assumptions, policy weight, invariant level sets, and finite-instrument population setting. Writing $d_k(x)=p_{k+1}(x)-p_k(x)$, monotonicity gives $Q_{\omega,k\mid x}(1-t)=\omega(x,p_k(x)+d_k(x)t)$ for Lebesgue-almost every $t\in(0,1)$. On each normalized slice $(\kappa_{j-1,k}(x),\kappa_{j,k}(x))$, this weight equals $\gamma_{\text{full},k}(x)+\gamma_{j,k}(x)$; after the last policy threshold, only the full-interval term remains. Reversing the outcome quantile yields the asserted upper representation, while its full-interval mean stays unchanged. On the tail, the weight is nonnegative and Fubini gives $\Delta_K(x)$. Independently differentiating the continuous component reproduces both displayed propensity representers, including the missing standalone lower-boundary constant when $j=0$; threshold changes leave only $O(t^2\delta\nu^2)$ under the stated density bounds. In the binary case, the separated branches give $\delta h_{j,k}^{-}=D_{j,k}^{-}(\delta P_{1,k+1}-\delta P_{1,k}-\delta p_{k+1})+I_{j,k}^{-}\delta q_{j,k}-E_{j,k}^{-}I_{j,k}^{-}\delta q_{j-1,k}$, exactly canceled by the printed residual corrections. Simplex-share directions contribute zero because policy values are tied at the truth. Denominator, product-weight, full-interval, and tail derivatives also cancel. Bounded admissible directions and overlap justify taking these derivatives through expectation. Retain $K\geqslant1$ for the tail denominator. \label{lem:orthogonality_discrete}
    Let $\eta_0$ denote the vector of true nuisance parameter values, let $\theta_0 = \underline{\theta}_{\omega,1}$,
and let $\mathcal{T}$ be the set of nuisance directions $\delta$ such that $\eta_0 + t\,\delta$ is an admissible nuisance value for all $t$ in a neighborhood of $0$.

\begin{enumerate}
        \item[\textup{(i)}] Under the hypotheses of \cref{thm:dml_normality}\textup{(i)}, the continuous-outcome score $\psi$ assembled in \cref{app:scores_continuous} satisfies

\[
            \mathbb{E}[\psi(O;\eta_0)] = \theta_0
            \qquad\text{and}\qquad

\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\psi(O;\eta_0 + t\,\delta)\bigr]\Big|_{t=0} = 0
            \quad

\text{for every } \delta \in \mathcal{T},
        \]

where $\theta_0$ is the target~(\ref{eq:target_discrete_iv}).
        \item[\textup{
(ii)}] Under the hypotheses of \cref{thm:dml_normality}\textup{(ii)}, the same two properties hold for the binary-outcome score~(\ref{eq:binary_score}),

with $\theta_0$ the target~(\ref{eq:binary_lower_bound}).
    \end{enumerate}

review.detail: The unqualified $L_2$ norm could denote population error over the marginal law of $X$ or empirical error on the fitting sample; the proof determines the population reading. Exact recovery gives feasible-oracle equality with probability tending to one, so using evaluation covariates for recovery does not invalidate the subsequent conditional argument. Expanding the continuous score reproduces denominator-regression products, product-weight errors, simplex-pooling products, and quadratic policy and quantile remainders. In the binary case, rearrangement preserves the rates, and branch errors have probability and expected contribution bounded by squared nuisance errors. These bounds give negligible conditional bias and score convergence; bounded clipped scores then establish the central limit and variance-consistency claims. Retain $K\geqslant1$ for the tail denominator. The lint warning is dismissed: the admissibility condition defines the directions quantified by the orthogonality lemma, rather than imposing another hypothesis on this theorem's fitted nuisances.
review.reading: Every nuisance-error norm in this theorem is the population norm $\|\hat f-f\|_{L_2}^2=\mathbb E_X[|\hat f(X)-f(X)|^2]$, with the fitted function held fixed during integration.

conditions.condition: $K\geqslant1$.
conditions.reason: The printed tail correction in $\psi_{\Delta_K}$ evaluates $1/\pi_K(X)$ at an observed positive-propensity level.

conditions.reason: Equation (\ref{eq:pf_cts_rank_kernel}) and its upper-bound analogue require feasible outcome-quantile values at exceptional randomized-rank endpoints.

conditions.reason: pins reading of ass:structure-consistency: Assumption \ref{asp:structure} states consistency as a structural equality of random variables; the subsequent observational derivation states conditional identities almost everywhere, consistently with the standard almost-sure convention.

The derivation preceding equation \ref{eq:canonical_submeasures} uses it to establish observational identities almost everywhere.

conditions.reason: pins reading of ass:structure-uniform-resistance: Assumption \ref{asp:structure} uses conditional-distribution notation without a pointwise covariate quantifier, while its common-support clause explicitly says every covariate value. The surrounding prose also recognizes that conditional probabilities are identified only almost surely.

conditions.condition: Any two structural laws satisfying Structural Assumptions and inducing the same $\mathbb P_{obs}$ give the same $\omega(x,u)$ for $\mathbb P_{obs}(\mathrm dx)\,\mathrm du$-almost every $(x,u)$.
conditions.reason: pins reading of ass:target-weight-identifiable: The paragraph following Structural Assumptions states that the observed law identifies conditional probabilities almost surely; equation (\ref{eq:omega_form}) constructs weights from such conditional expectations, and equation (\ref{eq:target_mte}) integrates against the covariate marginal and Lebesgue measure.

conditions.condition: The continuity condition holds for $\mathbb P_X$-almost every $x\in\mathcal X$.
conditions.reason: pins reading of ass:continuity-p-on-components: The prose preceding the conditional range decomposition specifies almost every covariate value under the observed law, and the proof of the Conditional General Bound disintegrates over the marginal law of the covariates.

conditions.condition: For every $z\in\mathcal Z$ and $x\in\mathcal X$, $p\mapsto\phi(z,x,p)$ is differentiable on $(0,1)$ and has finite right and left derivatives at $p=0$ and $p=1$, respectively; these are its endpoint values of $\partial\phi/\partial p$.
conditions.reason: pins reading of ass:phi-smooth-differentiable: The policy map has domain $\mathcal Z\times\mathcal X\times[0,1]$. The estimation procedure clips $\hat p$ to this interval, and the policy Taylor remainder in (\ref{eq:pf_dml_bias}) uses differentiation within that domain.

conditions.condition: There exist finite constants $C,L\geqslant0$ such that, for all $z\in\mathcal Z$, $x\in\mathcal X$, and $p,p'\in[0,1]$, $|\partial\phi/\partial p(z,x,p)|\leqslant C$ and $|\partial\phi/\partial p(z,x,p)-\partial\phi/\partial p(z,x,p')|\leqslant L|p-p'|$.
conditions.reason: pins reading of ass:phi-smooth-derivative: The exact-recovery argument for \cref{thm:dml_normality} uses a uniformly bounded derivative, and (\ref{eq:pf_dml_bias}) uses its uniformly Lipschitz derivative for the quadratic policy remainder.

conditions.condition: For every $x\in\mathcal X$ and every nonempty $T_{j,k}$, $\tau_{j,k}(x)\geqslant c_\pi$, where $c_\pi>0$ is the same constant used for $\pi_k$ in \cref{asp:overlap}.
conditions.reason: pins reading of ass:overlap-policy: Both clauses belong to the single quantified overlap assumption. The proof of \cref{thm:dml_normality} uses this assumption to bound the inverse-probability weights uniformly.

conditions.condition: For $\rho\in\{\mu,\nu\}$ and $t\in(0,1)$, $Q_\rho(t)=\inf\{a\in\mathbb R:\rho((\! -\infty,a])\geqslant t\}$.
conditions.reason: pins reading of ass:1d-ot-probability-laws: The standard generalized-inverse convention for probability quantiles applies to the notation section and Theorem~\ref{thm:1d_ot}; the theorem evaluates these functions at uniform draws and inside Lebesgue integrals.

conditions.condition: For each fixed $k\in\{0,\dots,K-1\}$ and $j\in\{0,\dots,l_k-1\}$ to which part~(i) is applied, its continuity hypothesis is $\mu_{1,k\mid X}(\{\nu_{j,k}(X)\})=\mu_{1,k\mid X}(\{\nu_{j+1,k}(X)\})=0$ almost surely under the marginal law of $X$.
conditions.reason: pins reading of ass:j-specialization-continuity: The proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:J_specialization}(i) fixes the band indices and uses continuity of the distribution function at the two boundaries to identify their probability levels and exclude boundary atoms.

conditions.condition: For a fresh $X$ with the population marginal law and independent of $I_1$, $\|\hat p(z,\cdot)-p(z,\cdot)\|_{L_2}^2=\mathbb E[(\hat p(z,X)-p(z,X))^2\mid I_1]$, and $n^{1/4}\max_{z\in\mathcal Z}\|\hat p(z,\cdot)-p(z,\cdot)\|_{L_2}\xrightarrow{P}0$ as $n\to\infty$.

\label{thm:dml_normality}
    Suppose \cref{asp:structure}, \cref{asp:phi_smooth}, \cref{asp:prop_gap},
and \cref{asp:overlap} hold and $\mathcal{Z}$ is finite.
Suppose the pre-recovery first stage fitted on $I_1$ satisfies $\max_{z\in\mathcal Z}\|\hat p(z,\cdot)-p(z,\cdot)\|_{L_2}=o_P(n^{-1/4})$.

Given the recovered level sets, suppose the remaining score nuisances fitted on $I_1$ are clipped to their known bounded ranges, every estimated conditional probability is clipped to $[0,1]$ before any difference is formed, $\hat\pi_k$ and $\hat\tau_{j,k}$ are clipped further to $[c_\pi/2,1]$,
and the estimators converge componentwise at rate $o_P(n^{-1/4})$ in $L_2$.
Suppose in addition that one of the following holds.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
        \item \textbf{Continuous outcome.} The nuisances include the boundary quantiles $\nu_{j,k}$,

and, uniformly in $X$, each relevant conditional law $Y\mid X,Z\in S_{k'},W=1$ has a density bounded in a fixed neighborhood of every true boundary $\nu_{j,k}(X)$, $j=1,\ldots,l_k$, for $k'=k+1$ and also for $k'=k$ when $k\geqslant1$;
at the fixed boundary $\nu_{0,k}=y_{\min}$, these conditional laws have no atom at $y_{\min}$.
\item \textbf{Discrete outcome.} The outcome is binary, \cref{asp:discrete_outcome_gap} holds,
and the nuisances are $p_k$, $P_{1,k}$, $\pi_k$, $\tau_{j,k}$, $a_{j,k}$, $\gamma_{\mathrm{full},k}$, $\gamma_{j,k}$,

and $\gamma_K$.
    \end{enumerate}
Then the sample-split estimator (\ref{eq:estimator_dml}) is $\sqrt{n}$-consistent and asymptotically normal:
where the asymptotic variance is the variance of the true orthogonal score, $\sigma^2 = \mathbb{E}\big[ ({\psi}(O; \eta) - \underline{\theta}_{\omega, 1})^2 \big]$.
It can be consistently estimated by its sample analog $\hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{1}{|I_2|} \sum_{i \in I_2} \big(\hat{\psi}(O_i; \hat{\eta}) - \hat{\underline{\theta}}_{\omega, 1}\big)^2$.

review.detail: The boundary quantile could denote the lower generalized inverse or a different inverse convention at flat portions of the cumulative distribution; the standard convention used by the referenced transport bound determines the former. On the initial gap, $\omega(x,u)$ is non-increasing, so its reversed weight quantile equals $\omega(x,\underline p(x)t)$ almost everywhere. Fubini then reproduces the negative boundary integral. Absolute continuity reproduces the clipped regression difference, with the two lower-endpoint terms cancelling. The nonnegative tail gives the displayed positive-part term. Reversing the boundary outcome quantile reproduces the upper bound. Compact outcome support bounds every integrand, and the explicit zero-boundary convention also covers singleton propensity supports.

\label{prop:continuous_reduction}
    Suppose \cref{asp:structure} and \cref{asp:continuity_p} hold,
and $\mathcal{Z}$ is connected.
Then the sharp lower bound in \cref{thm:covariate_continuous_lower_bound} admits the representation
where the first integral is defined as zero when $\underline{p}(X)=0$.
The sharp upper bound is obtained by replacing $Q_{1,\underline p\mid X}(v/\underline{p}(X))$ with $Q_{1,\underline p\mid X}(1-v/\underline{p}(X))$ and $y_{\min}$ with $y_{\max}$.

review.detail: Conditional on the training observations, clipping uniformly bounds the fitted integrand, so the independent evaluation average contributes $O_P(n^{-1/2})$. Independently decomposing the boundary error gives the endpoint contribution $C_Y(2|A'-A|+|D'-D|)$ plus $\underline p(X)W_1(\hat\mu_{1,\underline p\mid X},\mu_{1,\underline p\mid X})$, with $C_Y=\max\{|y_{\min}|,|y_{\max}|\}$. The endpoint bound remains valid when either scale is zero. The regression and tail errors are directly controlled by their stated target losses, yielding exactly the asserted rate. The theorem concerns the general plug-in estimator and requires no particular concrete learner construction.

\label{thm:continuous_rate}
    Suppose \cref{asp:structure}, \cref{asp:continuity_p},
and \cref{asp:continuous_rates} hold.

Then
    \[
        |\hat{\underline\theta}_{\omega,1}-\underline\theta_{\omega,1}|
        =O_P\!\left(n^{-1/2}+r_{e,n}+r_{g,n}+r_{\mu,n}\right).
    \]

review.detail: The algorithm, connected-instrument setting, learner conditions, and split regime are correctly carried. The lint warning is dismissed: \cref{asp:continuous_rates} is the conclusion established here, not an additional premise. At a flat piece of a distribution function, lower and upper generalized inverses can choose different quantiles; the standard lower generalized inverse fixes the population grid targets. The algorithm explicitly permits either printed interpolation-endpoint convention, and both satisfy the same rate. Independently reproducing the argument gives endpoint-map error $O_P(r_{p,n})$ and regression error $O_P(r_{g,\mathrm{loc},n}+r_{p,n})$, using the structural Lipschitz bound and nonexpansive projection. A selected treated law mixes population treated laws with $\underline p(x)\leqslant P\leqslant\underline p(x)+\delta_n+2\|\hat p-p\|_\infty$, so its weighted Wasserstein distance from the boundary law is at most $(y_{\max}-y_{\min})(\delta_n+2\|\hat p-p\|_\infty)$. Sorting contracts the full grid error after the excluded-grid errors are bounded; interpolation contributes a telescoping variation term of order $M_Q^{-1}$. Thus the boundary-law rate contains exactly $r_{Q,n}+\delta_n+r_{p,n}+\varepsilon_n+M_Q^{-1}$. The zero-boundary and zero-selection conventions close those cases, and substitution into the binding \cref{thm:continuous_rate} yields the displayed estimator rate.

\label{cor:continuous_primitive_rate}
    Suppose \cref{asp:structure} and \cref{asp:continuity_p} hold.
Suppose additionally that $\phi$ is uniformly Lipschitz in its last argument: for some $L_\phi<\infty$,

\[
        |\phi(z,x,p')-\phi(z,x,p)|\leqslant L_\phi|p'-p|
    \]
for all $(z,x,p,p')\in\mathcal Z\times\mathcal X\times[0,1]^2$.
Suppose that \cref{asp:continuous_learners} holds with rates $r_{p,n}$, $r_{g,\mathrm{loc},n}$, $r_{Q,n}$ and trimming sequence $\varepsilon_n$,
that $|I_j|/n\to\rho_j\in(0,1)$ for $j=0,1,2$,

and that
    \[
        r_{p,n},\ r_{g,\mathrm{loc},n},\ r_{Q,n},\ \delta_n,\ \varepsilon_n,\ M_Q^{-1}\longrightarrow0.
    \]
Then the nuisance estimators produced by \cref{alg:continuous_instrument} satisfy \cref{asp:continuous_rates} with

\[
    \begin{aligned}
        r_{e,n}&=O(r_{p,n}),\\
        r_{g,n}&=O\!\left(r_{g,\mathrm{loc},n}+r_{p,n}\right),\\
        r_{\mu,n}&=O\!\left(
          r_{Q,n}+\delta_n+r_{p,n}+\varepsilon_n+M_Q^{-1}\right).
    \end{aligned}
    \]

and consequently
    \[
        |\hat{\underline\theta}_{\omega,1}-\underline\theta_{\omega,1}|
        =O_P\!\left(n^{-1/2}+r_{p,n}+r_{g,\mathrm{loc},n}
        +r_{Q,n}+\delta_n+\varepsilon_n+M_Q^{-1}\right).
    \]

defRow.code: IsDMLProcedure S I₁ I₂ pHat phi dphi rho gap eHat firstStage regression multinomial moment cpi theta : Prop

segments.text: Following the standard DML template, we randomly partition the sample into an auxiliary set $I_1$ and a main estimation set $I_2$.
On $I_1$ we estimate the propensity score $p$, clip it to $[0,1]$,
and set $\hat q=\phi(\cdot,\cdot,\hat p)$;

using only the covariates in $I_2$, we average $\hat p$ and $\hat q$ over $X$ and recover the level sets $\widehat S_k$ and $\widehat T_{j,k}$ as connected components of the graph that joins two averaged values lying within $c_{\mathrm{gap}}/2$ of each other.

Given those sets we fit the remaining nuisances on $I_1$---the interval boundaries $\hat p_k$, the probability weights $\hat\gamma$, $\hat\pi_k$, $\hat\tau_{j,k}$ and within-set shares $\hat a_{j,k}$, the boundary quantiles $\hat\nu_{j,k}$,
and the conditional expectations $\hat M^{\pm}_{j,k}$, $\hat J^{\pm}_{j,k}$, $\hat J^{\pm}_{\mathrm{full},k}$---clipping each to its known range,
and finally average the plug-in orthogonal scores over $I_2$ to form~(\ref{eq:estimator_dml}).
\cref{alg:dml_continuous_outcome} states the procedure step by step;
the explicit graph construction, the moment equation defining $\nu_{j,k}$, the conditional-expectation components,
and the Neyman-orthogonal scores $\psi^{\mathrm{prod}}$ are given in \cref{app:procedure_continuous_outcome} and \cref{app:scores_continuous}.

defRow.code: IsDMLContinuousAlgorithm S I₁ I₂ pHat phi dphi rho gap eHat firstStage regression multinomial moment cpi theta variance : Prop

segments.text: \STATE Split sample into $I_1$ (auxiliary) and $I_2$ (main).
\STATE \textbf{On $I_1$:} estimate propensity $\hat p(z,x)$, clip it to $[0,1]$,
and set $\hat q(z,x) = \phi(z,x,\hat p(z,x))$.
\STATE \textbf{Using the covariates in $I_2$:} form $\bar p_2(z)=|I_2|^{-1}\sum_{i\in I_2}\hat p(z,X_i)$
and $\bar q_2(z)=|I_2|^{-1}\sum_{i\in I_2}\hat q(z,X_i)$.
Assign structural-zero categories to $\widehat S_0$ as in Step~1 below and remove their baseline vertices.

Connect two remaining labeled values when their distance is less than $c_{\mathrm{gap}}/2$ and take graph connected components to obtain and order the positive-baseline sets $\widehat S_k$ and the policy sets $\widehat T_{j,k}$.
\STATE \textbf{On $I_1$, given the recovered sets:} set $\hat p_0\equiv0$ and, for $k\geqslant1$, estimate $\hat p_k(x)=\widehat{\mathbb E}[W\mid Z\in\widehat S_k,X=x]$.
Estimate the two conditional probabilities defining $\gamma_{\mathrm{full},k}(x)$ from their set indicators and subtract them;
estimate $\hat\pi_k(x)$, $\hat\tau_{j,k}(x)$, $\hat\gamma_{j,k}(x)$,
and $\hat\gamma_K(x)$ from the corresponding set indicators.
Clip all estimated conditional probabilities to $[0,1]$ and $\hat\pi_k,\hat\tau_{j,k}$ further to $[c_\pi/2,1]$.
Within each $\widehat T_{j,k}$, estimate the shares $\{\hat a_{j,k}(z,x):z\in\widehat T_{j,k}\}$ jointly with a simplex-valued multinomial learner, so they are nonnegative and sum to one,
and set $\hat q_{j,k}(x)=\sum_{z\in\widehat T_{j,k}}\hat a_{j,k}(z,x)\hat q(z,x)$.
\STATE Estimate boundary quantiles $\hat\nu_{j,k}(x)$ via the moment-equation regression in Step~4 below and clip them to $[y_{\min},y_{\max}]$.

\STATE Estimate conditional expectations $\hat M_{j,k}^{\pm}(x)$, $\hat J_{j,k}^{\pm}(x)$, $\hat J_{\mathrm{full},k}^{\pm}(x)$ by flexible ML, omitting every minus-side object at the structural boundary $k=0$.
\STATE \textbf{On $I_2$:} compute orthogonal scores $\hat\psi^{\mathrm{prod}}_{\mathrm{full},k}, \hat\psi^{\mathrm{prod}}_{j,k}, \hat\psi_{\Delta_K}$ from \cref{app:scores_continuous}.
\STATE Return $\hat{\underline\theta}_{\omega,1}$ as in~(\ref{eq:estimator_dml}) and $\hat\sigma^2 = |I_2|^{-1}\sum_{i\in I_2}(\hat\psi(O_i;\hat\eta) - \hat{\underline\theta}_{\omega,1})^2$.

ass:domains-compact-borel.says: Throughout the paper, we assume that all domains are compact, carry their Borel $\sigma$-fields, and are standard Borel spaces.

ass:outcome-endpoints-known.says: we treat the outcome domain and hence its feasible endpoints as known.

ass:structure-instrument-exogeneity.says: \item (Conditional Instrumental Exogeneity) $Z \indep (U,Y(0),Y(1)) \mid X$, where $\indep$ denotes statistical independence.

ass:structure-common-support.says: \item (Common Instrument Support) The conditional support of $Z$ given $X$ does not depend on $X$: $\mathrm{Supp}(Z \mid X=x) = \mathcal{Z}$ for all $x \in \mathcal{X}$.

ass:target-weight-measurable.says: The function $\omega:\mathcal X\times[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ is jointly measurable

ass:continuity-p-components.says:
\label{asp:continuity_p}
    The instrument domain $\mathcal{Z}$ has finitely many connected components.

ass:continuity-p-on-components.says: For almost every $x \in \mathcal{X}$, the conditional propensity score function $z \mapsto p(z,x) = \mathbb{P}(W=1 \mid Z=z, X=x)$ is continuous on each connected component.

ass:phi-smooth-differentiable.says: The map $\phi(z,x,p)$ is differentiable with respect to $p$,

ass:phi-smooth-derivative.says: $\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial p}$ is bounded and uniformly Lipschitz in $p$ for all $z \in \mathcal{Z}$ and $x \in \mathcal{X}$.

ass:prop-gap-separation.says: \item There exists a constant $c_{\text{gap}} > 0$ such that, for all $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and all $v,v' \in R_x = \{p(z,x),q(z,x)\}_{z \in \mathcal{Z}}$, either $v'=v$ or $|v-v'|>c_{\text{gap}}$.

ass:prop-gap-invariant-order.says: Moreover, the equality classes and their strict ordering are invariant in $x$: the sets $S_k$, $T_{j,k}$ and their indices $K,l_k$ do not depend on $x$.

ass:prop-gap-boundary-distinct.says: \item For every $k=0,\ldots,K-1$ and every nonempty $T_{j,k}$, $q_{j,k}(x)\neq p_k(x)$ for all $x$.

ass:overlap-baseline.says: There exists a constant $c_\pi > 0$ such that $\pi_k(x) \geqslant c_\pi$ for every $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and observed positive-propensity level $k \in \{1, \dots, K\}$,

ass:overlap-policy.says: $\tau_{j,k}(x)\geqslant c_\pi$ for every nonempty alternative-policy level set $T_{j,k}$.

ass:discrete-outcome-gap.says:
\label{asp:discrete_outcome_gap}
    There exists $c_h>0$ such that, for every $k=0,\ldots,K-1$ with $l_k\geqslant1$ and $j=0,\ldots,l_k$, almost surely,
    \[
    \left|p_{k+1}(X)-J_{\mathrm{full},k}(X)-q_{j,k}(X)\right|\geqslant c_h.
    \]

ass:1d-ot-probability-laws.says:
\label{thm:1d_ot}
    Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on $\mathbb{R}$ with quantile functions $Q_\mu$ and $Q_\nu$.

ass:1d-ot-moment-support.says: Suppose either that $\mu$ has bounded support and $\nu$ has a finite first moment, or vice versa,

ass:1d-ot-product-cost.says: let the cost be the simple product $c(a,b) = a \cdot b$.

ass:sharpness-observed-model.says:
\label{prop:sharpness}
    Suppose the observed distribution $\mathbb{P}_{obs}$ is generated by a true structural model satisfying \cref{asp:structure}.

ass:j-specialization-continuity.says: If $\mu_{1,k\mid X}$ is continuous at $\nu_{j,k}(X)$ and $\nu_{j+1,k}(X)$ almost surely,

ass:dml-normality-first-stage.says: Suppose the pre-recovery first stage fitted on $I_1$ satisfies $\max_{z\in\mathcal Z}\|\hat p(z,\cdot)-p(z,\cdot)\|_{L_2}=o_P(n^{-1/4})$.

ass:dml-normality-score-clipping.says: Given the recovered level sets, suppose the remaining score nuisances fitted on $I_1$ are clipped to their known bounded ranges,

ass:dml-normality-probability-clipping.says: every estimated conditional probability is clipped to $[0,1]$ before any difference is formed,

ass:dml-normality-nuisance-rates.says: the estimators converge componentwise at rate $o_P(n^{-1/4})$ in $L_2$.

ass:dml-normality-continuous-nuisances.says: The nuisances include the boundary quantiles $\nu_{j,k}$,

ass:dml-normality-boundary-densities.says: uniformly in $X$, each relevant conditional law $Y\mid X,Z\in S_{k'},W=1$ has a density bounded in a fixed neighborhood of every true boundary $\nu_{j,k}(X)$, $j=1,\ldots,l_k$, for $k'=k+1$ and also for $k'=k$ when $k\geqslant1$;

ass:dml-normality-no-lower-atom.says: at the fixed boundary $\nu_{0,k}=y_{\min}$, these conditional laws have no atom at $y_{\min}$.

ass:connected-instrument-domain.says: We now consider a connected instrument domain $\mathcal Z$.

ass:continuous-split-proportions.says: We use three-way sample splitting with $|I_j|/n\to\rho_j\in(0,1)$ for $j=0,1,2$

ass:continuous-rates-endpoints.says:
\item Each of the three maps entering the boundary integral and the trivial tail,
        \begin{equation*}
            \Lambda \;\in\; \Bigl\{\ \underline{p}(X),\ \ \min\{\underline{p}(X),\,q(Z,X)\},\ \ \bigl(q(Z,X)-\overline{p}(X)\bigr)_+ \ \Bigr\},
        \end{equation*}
        satisfies
        \[
            \mathbb E_{Z,X}\!\left[\,\bigl|\hat\Lambda-\Lambda\bigr|\ \middle|\ I_0,I_1\right]=O_P(r_{e,n}),
        \]
        with $r_{e,n}\to0$.

ass:continuous-rates-regression.says:
\item The clipped estimator $\hat g_1$ satisfies the target-evaluation rate
        \begin{multline*}
            \mathbb E_{Z,X}\Bigl[
              |\hat g_1(\hat q^{\mathrm{tr}}(Z,X),X)-g_1(q^{\mathrm{tr}}(Z,X),X)| \\
              +|\hat g_1(\hat P,X)-g_1(P,X)|
              \ \Bigm|\ I_0,I_1\Bigr]=O_P(r_{g,n}).
        \end{multline*}

ass:continuous-rates-boundary-law.says:
It satisfies the target-weighted rate
        \[
            \mathbb E_X\!\left[\underline{p}(X)W_1\!\left(\hat\mu_{1,\underline p\mid X},\mu_{1,\underline p\mid X}\right)\ \middle|\ I_0,I_1\right]=O_P(r_{\mu,n}).
        \]

ass:continuous-learners-outcome.says:
\item \textbf{Outcome learner.} The fitted learner satisfies the target prediction rate
    \[

def:dml-estimation-procedure.says: Following the standard DML template, we randomly partition the sample into an auxiliary set $I_1$ and a main estimation set $I_2$. On $I_1$ we estimate the propensity score $p$, clip it to $[0,1]$, and set $\hat q=\phi(\cdot,\cdot,\hat p)$; using only the covariates in $I_2$, we average $\hat p$ and $\hat q$ over $X$ and recover the level sets $\widehat S_k$ and $\widehat T_{j,k}$ as connected components of the graph that joins two averaged values lying within $c_{\mathrm{gap}}/2$ of each other. Given those sets we fit the remaining nuisances on $I_1$---the interval boundaries $\hat p_k$, the probability weights $\hat\gamma$, $\hat\pi_k$, $\hat\tau_{j,k}$ and within-set shares $\hat a_{j,k}$, the boundary quantiles $\hat\nu_{j,k}$, and the conditional expectations $\hat M^{\pm}_{j,k}$, $\hat J^{\pm}_{j,k}$, $\hat J^{\pm}_{\mathrm{full},k}$---clipping each to its known range, and finally average the plug-in orthogonal scores over $I_2$ to form~(\ref{eq:estimator_dml}). \cref{alg:dml_continuous_outcome} states the procedure step by step; the explicit graph construction, the moment equation defining $\nu_{j,k}$, the conditional-expectation components, and the Neyman-orthogonal scores $\psi^{\mathrm{prod}}$ are given in \cref{app:procedure_continuous_outcome} and \cref{app:scores_continuous}.

def:dml-continuous-outcome-algorithm.says:
\STATE Split sample into $I_1$ (auxiliary) and $I_2$ (main).
\STATE \textbf{On $I_1$:} estimate propensity $\hat p(z,x)$, clip it to $[0,1]$, and set $\hat q(z,x) = \phi(z,x,\hat p(z,x))$.
\STATE \textbf{Using the covariates in $I_2$:} form $\bar p_2(z)=|I_2|^{-1}\sum_{i\in I_2}\hat p(z,X_i)$ and $\bar q_2(z)=|I_2|^{-1}\sum_{i\in I_2}\hat q(z,X_i)$. Assign structural-zero categories to $\widehat S_0$ as in Step~1 below and remove their baseline vertices. Connect two remaining labeled values when their distance is less than $c_{\mathrm{gap}}/2$ and take graph connected components to obtain and order the positive-baseline sets $\widehat S_k$ and the policy sets $\widehat T_{j,k}$.
\STATE \textbf{On $I_1$, given the recovered sets:} set $\hat p_0\equiv0$ and, for $k\geqslant1$, estimate $\hat p_k(x)=\widehat{\mathbb E}[W\mid Z\in\widehat S_k,X=x]$. Estimate the two conditional probabilities defining $\gamma_{\mathrm{full},k}(x)$ from their set indicators and subtract them; estimate $\hat\pi_k(x)$, $\hat\tau_{j,k}(x)$, $\hat\gamma_{j,k}(x)$, and $\hat\gamma_K(x)$ from the corresponding set indicators. Clip all estimated conditional probabilities to $[0,1]$ and $\hat\pi_k,\hat\tau_{j,k}$ further to $[c_\pi/2,1]$. Within each $\widehat T_{j,k}$, estimate the shares $\{\hat a_{j,k}(z,x):z\in\widehat T_{j,k}\}$ jointly with a simplex-valued multinomial learner, so they are nonnegative and sum to one, and set $\hat q_{j,k}(x)=\sum_{z\in\widehat T_{j,k}}\hat a_{j,k}(z,x)\hat q(z,x)$.
\STATE Estimate boundary quantiles $\hat\nu_{j,k}(x)$ via the moment-equation regression in Step~4 below and clip them to $[y_{\min},y_{\max}]$.
\STATE Estimate conditional expectations $\hat M_{j,k}^{\pm}(x)$, $\hat J_{j,k}^{\pm}(x)$, $\hat J_{\mathrm{full},k}^{\pm}(x)$ by flexible ML, omitting every minus-side object at the structural boundary $k=0$.
\STATE \textbf{On $I_2$:} compute orthogonal scores $\hat\psi^{\mathrm{prod}}_{\mathrm{full},k}, \hat\psi^{\mathrm{prod}}_{j,k}, \hat\psi_{\Delta_K}$ from \cref{app:scores_continuous}.
\STATE Return $\hat{\underline\theta}_{\omega,1}$ as in~(\ref{eq:estimator_dml}) and $\hat\sigma^2 = |I_2|^{-1}\sum_{i\in I_2}(\hat\psi(O_i;\hat\eta) - \hat{\underline\theta}_{\omega,1})^2$.
