paper.title: Partial Identification of Policy-Relevant Treatment Effects with Instrumental Variables via Optimal Transport
paper.authors: Jiyuan Tan, Jose Blanchet, Vasilis Syrgkanis
paper.html:
Abstract

Policy-Relevant Treatment Effects (PRTEs) are generally not point-identified under standard instrumental variable (IV) assumptions when the instrument generates limited support in treatment propensity. Existing approaches optimize over marginal treatment response functions subject to moment restrictions and can discard identifying distributional information. We show that PRTE partial identification in the generalized Roy model can instead be formulated as a Constrained Conditional Optimal Transport (CCOT) problem, which reduces analytically to separable one-dimensional OT problems with product costs, yielding sharp closed-form bounds. We also develop estimation and inference procedures: for discrete instruments, a Double Machine Learning approach based on Neyman-orthogonal scores that accommodates high-dimensional covariates while achieving the parametric n​ rate and asymptotic normality; for continuous instruments, we characterize the nonparametric convergence rates. The framework accommodates covariates as well as discrete and continuous instruments. In simulations and a bed-net subsidy application, our bounds are substantially tighter than existing moment-relaxation methods.

1 Introduction

Instrumental variables (IVs) are a standard tool for identifying causal effects when treatment assignment is endogenous in observational studies. Under the classical IV assumptions, Angrist and Imbens (1995) show that the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE), defined as the average effect for the subpopulation of compliers, is point-identified. However, many policy questions are not about compliers themselves; they ask how outcomes would change under a counterfactual policy that shifts treatment take-up in the broader population. Such questions are naturally captured by Policy-Relevant Treatment Effects (PRTEs), which are central targets in the generalized Roy and Marginal Treatment Effect (MTE) framework [Heckman and Vytlacil, 1999; Heckman and Vytlacil, 2005; Heckman et~al., 2006]. This framework encompasses a wide range of causal estimands, including the Average Treatment Effect (ATE); empirical policy evaluations within it include Carneiro et~al. (2010); Carneiro et~al. (2011). Unlike LATE, PRTEs are generally not point-identified when the instrument induces only limited support in the treatment propensity.
This limited-support problem is central in the generalized Roy model [Heckman and Vytlacil, 2005], where treatment selection follows a threshold-crossing mechanism formally equivalent to the classical monotonicity condition [Angrist and Imbens, 1995; Vytlacil, 2002]. In this framework, PRTEs can be written as weighted averages of the MTE, so identification depends on how much of the latent resistance distribution is reached by the propensity score induced by the instrument. When the propensity score lacks full support on the unit interval, PRTEs and related quantities such as the ATE remain only partially identified, and a long line of work has studied such identified sets under various assumptions [Manski, 1990; Manski, 1997; Manski and Pepper, 2000; Heckman and Vytlacil, 2001; Mogstad et~al., 2018].
Despite its importance, deriving tight, closed-form bounds for general PRTEs remains a significant challenge. Existing strategies fall into three broad approaches: moment-relaxation over MTR functions [Mogstad et~al., 2018; Mogstad and Torgovitsky, 2018], second-order stochastic dominance constraints on the MTE function solved by rearrangement [Marx, 2024], and infinite-dimensional linear programming over the joint law of outcome and latent resistance solved by sieve approximation [Han and Yang, 2024]. Each faces limitations—discarded distributional information, restricted scope to weights on the complier interval under a binary instrument, lack of closed-form solutions or incompatibility with continuous instruments—that we discuss in detail in 1.1.
In this paper, we develop a unified Optimal Transport (OT) framework for partial identification in the generalized Roy model and use it to derive sharp, closed-form bounds for PRTEs. Specifically, we recast PRTE partial identification as a Constrained Conditional Optimal Transport (CCOT) problem, a structured instance within the broader OT framework that is equivalent to the infinite-dimensional LP of Han and Yang (2024). Rather than summarizing the observed distributions through moment conditions or imposing distributional constraints on conditional mean (MTE) functions, we place the distributional constraints directly on the joint conditional law of the potential outcome and latent resistance. Then, we exploit the OT structure to prove that this heavily constrained, multidimensional CCOT problem analytically reduces to separable one-dimensional OT problems. This reduction completely bypasses computationally intensive linear programming and sieve approximation, yielding explicit, closed-form solutions for the sharp bounds.
Our main contributions can be summarized as follows.
  1. A Unified OT Framework for the Generalized Roy Model: We formulate partial identification in the generalized Roy model as a CCOT problem. The framework imposes distributional constraints directly at the joint-law level, and we prove that the constraints decompose analytically into separable marginal constraints.
  2. Analytic Decomposition and Closed-Form PRTE Bounds: Leveraging the decomposition, we prove the CCOT problem decomposes into separable one-dimensional OT problems with product costs, yielding explicit, closed-form sharp bounds and bypassing the sieve approximation required by existing computational approaches.
  3. Semiparametric Estimation and Inference: We develop estimation results for the binary-treatment bounds. For discrete instruments, we leverage Double Machine Learning (DML) to construct a debiased estimator, achieving n​-consistency and asymptotic normality. For continuous instruments, we explicitly characterize the nonparametric convergence rates.
  4. Empirical Validation: We validate our theoretical results through both synthetic simulations and a real-world empirical application, demonstrating how our closed-form bounds tighten the identified set relative to the moment-relaxation methods.
Replacing threshold crossing by a conditional quantile representation of the selection equation yields sharp closed-form bounds for continuous and multi-valued treatments, under a rank-overlap condition and an algebraic condition on the instrument-induced latent intervals, respectively. A companion note develops those results in full; the present paper treats the binary case throughout.
Organization of this paper. 2 introduces the setup and optimal transport background; 3 presents the main identification theory and closed-form bounds; 4 develops estimation and inference; and 5 reports simulation and empirical results. The main identification and inference proofs, the algorithms, and the orthogonal score formulas are in the Appendix; the Online Appendix collects the notation table, worked examples, supporting derivations, and full simulation and empirical documentation.

1.1 Related Work

Local IV and MTE. The Marginal Treatment Effect (MTE) of Heckman and Vytlacil (1999); Heckman and Vytlacil (2005) is the building block of our identification analysis: it is the treatment effect at a given quantile of unobserved resistance, and all standard IV estimands—LATE, ATE, ATT, and PRTE—are weighted averages of it [Heckman and Vytlacil, 2005; Heckman et~al., 2006]. Vytlacil (2002) establishes the equivalence between the threshold-crossing selection model and the monotonicity assumption of Angrist and Imbens (1995). Point identification proceeds via the Local Instrumental Variables (LIV) estimand [Heckman and Vytlacil, 1999], which requires full propensity score support over [0,1]—the condition that fails under limited instrument variation, the regime our paper addresses.
Partial Identification. Manski (1990); Manski (1997); Manski and Pepper (2000) pioneered partial identification, providing closed-form bounds for the IV problem under a range of assumptions; as a special case, our bound recovers the classical Manski bound for the ATE. In the econometric literature, partial identification is often cast as estimating the identified set defined by moment inequalities [Chernozhukov et~al., 2007]; see Tamer (2010) for a comprehensive survey.
Balke and Pearl (1997) develop the linear programming approach for partial identification, which has recently been revisited and generalized using modern techniques [Balazadeh~Meresht et~al., 2022; Guo et~al., 2022; Duarte et~al., 2024; Levis et~al., 2025]; in particular, Levis et~al. (2025) use covariates to tighten the classical bound of Balke and Pearl (1997) and develop estimation theory in the IV setting. Several works connect partial identification to robust optimization [Guo et~al., 2022; Balazadeh~Meresht et~al., 2022; Fan et~al., 2025; Tan et~al., 2024], and, in settings without unmeasured confounding, the problem can be formulated as an optimal transport problem with marginal constraints derived from the observed-data distribution [Ji et~al., 2024; Lin et~al., 2025{a}; Lin et~al., 2025{b}]; see Gunsilius (2025) for a recent primer. In related but distinct settings, Fan et~al. (2017) study partial identification of functionals of the joint distribution of potential outcomes when the conditional marginals are identified, and Ober-Reynolds (2023) characterizes sharp bounds on functionals of the joint complier outcome distribution via optimal transport under the binary-instrument LATE framework of Angrist and Imbens (1995). The first bounds functionals of the joint law from identified marginals, the second an identified subpopulation; neither addresses the PRTE weights we study here.
PRTE Partial Identification. Three strategies have emerged for PRTE partial identification under limited support. Mogstad et~al. (2018) optimize over MTR functions subject to moment constraints [Mogstad and Torgovitsky, 2018]. This moment relaxation discards distributional information beyond the first moment. Han and Yang (2024) preserve full distributional content by formulating an infinite-dimensional LP over the joint law of latent states, solved by sieve approximation for discrete instruments. Marx (2024) generalizes the approach of Mogstad et~al. (2018) by imposing full distributional content on the MTE function via a second-order stochastic dominance (SSD) constraint, obtaining sharp closed-form bounds by rearrangement; the paper's explicit theorems cover weights on the complier interval under a binary instrument, with extensions beyond compliers requiring rank similarity.
Our work differs from all three in scope: we impose distributional constraints directly on the joint conditional law of the potential outcome and latent resistance rather than on a conditional mean, cast the resulting program as a CCOT problem equivalent to the LP of Han and Yang (2024), and show it reduces analytically to separable one-dimensional OT problems with product costs. This delivers (i) sharp closed-form bounds for the full PRTE on all of [0,1] under multi-valued instruments via an interval decomposition across K+1 compliance types, including boundary intervals where only one potential outcome marginal is identified, (ii) extensions to continuous and mixed instruments with sub-problems indexed by the propensity score continuum, and (iii) discrete-instrument inference together with continuous-instrument rate results, which are limited in either Marx (2024) or Han and Yang (2024). On the complier interval under a binary instrument, the CCOT solution and the SSD rearrangement of Marx (2024) coincide. Beyond PRTE, our sharpness result characterizes the identified set at the level of the full joint latent law and sheds light on the joint-identification question raised in Marx (2024) through its reduction to independent one-dimensional marginal constraints.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 IV Model and Policy-Relevant Treatment Effects

For most of this paper, we work with the generalized Roy model [Heckman and Vytlacil, 2005]. In the model, the observable variables are treatment W∈W={0,1}, instrument Z∈Z, covariates X∈X, and outcome Y∈Y, where X⊂RdX​, Z, and Y⊂R are the domains of the corresponding variables. We consider both discrete and continuous instrument settings in this paper. Throughout the paper, we assume that all domains are compact, carry their Borel σ-fields, and are standard Borel spaces. Write ymin​=minY and ymax​=maxY; compactness guarantees that these extrema exist, and we treat the outcome domain and hence its feasible endpoints as known. The unobservables are the potential outcomes Y(0),Y(1), and the variable U in the selection equation (2.1). Thus, Z is the instrument, W is the treatment, X is observed covariate information, Y is the observed outcome, and U is an unobserved latent resistance variable.
Assumption 2.1 (Structural Assumptions).
We impose the following structural assumptions on our IV model. Throughout, we assume Y(w)∈Y almost surely.
  1. (Consistency) Y=WY(1)+(1−W)Y(0).
  2. (Conditional Instrumental Exogeneity) Z⊥⊥(U,Y(0),Y(1))∣X, where ⊥⊥ denotes statistical independence.
  3. (Threshold Crossing) The treatment is selected by
    W=1(U⩽p(Z,X)),​​(2.1)​
    where p(Z,X)=P(W=1∣Z,X). Moreover, U∣X∼Unif(0,1).
  4. (Common Instrument Support) The conditional support of Z given X does not depend on X: Supp(Z∣X=x)=Z for all x∈X.
Because Y(w)∈Y and Y is compact, ymin​⩽Y(w)⩽ymax​ almost surely; boundedness therefore follows from the maintained setup. It is without loss of generality to impose U∣X∼Unif(0,1) when the original latent resistance has a continuous conditional distribution, because we can normalize that distribution.1Let V denote the original latent resistance, let c(Z,X) be its cutoff, and suppose FV∣X​(⋅∣x) is continuous. Define U~=FV∣X​(V∣X) and the transformed cutoff p~​(z,x)=FV∣X​(c(z,x)∣x). The conditional probability integral transform gives U~∣X∼Unif(0,1), and 1{V⩽c(Z,X)}=1{U~⩽p~​(Z,X)} almost surely. The common instrument support condition lets us use the same instrument domain at each covariate value. The observed law identifies conditional probabilities almost surely; the continuity condition introduced in Assumption 3.6 selects their continuous propensity-score version throughout the conditional support.
The fundamental building block for evaluating causal parameters in this framework is the MTE, originally introduced by Heckman and Vytlacil (1999); Heckman and Vytlacil (2005). The MTE is defined as the average treatment effect for individuals with covariates X=x and latent variable U=u:
MTE(x,u)=E[Y(1)−Y(0)∣X=x,U=u].
In policy analysis, we are often interested in the effect of an intervention that changes treatment take-up from a baseline status to a new regime. Let the baseline policy be characterized by the current propensity score p(Z,X) and the corresponding treatment status W. Consider an alternative policy that induces a counterfactual propensity score q(Z,X) and a new treatment status Wq=1(U⩽q(Z,X)), where we assume the latent variable U is invariant to the policy change, as is standard in the MTE framework.
The PRTE evaluates the average per-person impact of shifting from the baseline policy to the alternative policy. Define the outcome realized under the alternative policy by Yq=WqY(1)+(1−Wq)Y(0). The PRTE is formally defined as
PRTE=E[Wq−W]E[Yq−Y]​.
Many common treatment effect parameters can be expressed as a weighted average of the MTE. Specifically, the PRTE can be rewritten as:
PRTE=EX,U​[MTE(X,U)ωPRTE​(X,U)],
where the policy-specific weight function is given by:
ωPRTE​(x,u)=E[q(Z,X)−p(Z,X)]P(q(Z,X)⩾u∣X=x)−P(p(Z,X)⩾u∣X=x)​,
provided E[q(Z,X)−p(Z,X)]=0. Following Heckman and Vytlacil (2005); Mogstad et~al. (2018), we consider the following more general target parameter.
θω​=EX​∫01​MTE(X,u)ω(X,u)du,​​(2.2)​
where ω is the target-specific weight. We impose the following standing condition on this weight.
Assumption 2.2 (Target-Weight Regularity).
The function ω:X×[0,1]→R is jointly measurable and identifiable from the observed law, and
EX​[∫01​∣ω(X,u)∣du]<∞.
Together with the compact outcome domain, Assumption 2.2 ensures that θω​ is finite. We can obtain different PRTEs by taking
ω(x,u)∝E[1(u⩽q1​(Z,X))−1(u⩽q0​(Z,X))∣X=x],​​(2.3)​
for given propensity functions q0​ and q1​, where q0​=p and q1​=q correspond to the baseline and alternative propensity score functions, respectively, in the PRTE case. The coefficient hidden inside the proportionality symbol is identifiable. 1 shows a variety of common causal parameters under different choices of ω.
While our bounds recover the classical bounds for the first four quantities in 1, we focus in particular on PRTEs. As a leading example, consider a uniform policy shift of the form q(Z,X)=min(p(Z,X)+α,1) for some α>0. This corresponds to a policy that uniformly raises the probability of treatment uptake by α. In our empirical application (5), the instrument is the offered price of an insecticide-treated bed net [Dupas, 2014], and q=p+α models a uniform price subsidy that lowers the cost of purchase and thereby increases take-up probability by α.
Heckman and Vytlacil (2001) shows that if the support of p(Z,x) spans the entire interval (0,1) for all x, then the MTE is identifiable. However, because the common support of p(Z,X) is often a strict subset of (0,1), the MTE is generally not identifiable. For instance, when both X and Z are discrete, the supports of p(Z,x) are discrete and this full-support condition is violated.

2.2 A Primer on Optimal Transport

To build the framework for our partial identification results, we briefly introduce the relevant concepts from OT theory. OT provides a mathematical framework for coupling two probability distributions at minimum cost, and has emerged as a powerful toolkit for bounding joint distributions when only their marginals are known [Galichon, 2016].
Let μ and ν be two probability measures on state spaces A and B, respectively. In the context of partial identification, we often observe the marginal distributions of two variables but not their joint distribution. We define Π(μ,ν) as the set of all couplings between μ and ν. Formally, a coupling π∈Π(μ,ν) is a joint probability measure on the product space A×B such that its marginals are exactly μ and ν.
Given a cost function c:A×B→R∪{+∞} that represents the cost of associating state a with state b, the standard Kantorovich optimal transport problem seeks the coupling that minimizes the expected cost:
π∈Π(μ,ν)inf​∫A×B​c(a,b)dπ(a,b).​​(2.4)​
Generally, solving (2.4) in multidimensional spaces requires computationally intensive linear programming. However, a celebrated result in the OT literature demonstrates that when the spaces are one-dimensional and the cost function satisfies specific structural conditions—such as supermodularity—the optimal coupling admits a sharp, closed-form solution.
We formalize this one-dimensional closed-form solution in the following theorem, which we use to derive the analytic PRTE bounds.
Theorem 2.3 (1D Optimal Transport with Product Cost; see, e.g., [Villani, 2021; Galichon, 2016]).
Let μ and ν be probability measures on R with quantile functions Qμ​ and Qν​. Suppose either that μ has bounded support and ν has a finite first moment, or vice versa, and let the cost be the simple product c(a,b)=a⋅b. Then, the minimum and maximum of the expected cost over all valid couplings are completely characterized by the countermonotonic and comonotonic couplings, respectively:
π∈Π(μ,ν)min​∫R2​a⋅bdπ(a,b)π∈Π(μ,ν)max​∫R2​a⋅bdπ(a,b)​=∫01​Qμ​(t)Qν​(1−t)dt,=∫01​Qμ​(t)Qν​(t)dt.​
The minimum is attained by the countermonotonic coupling (Qμ​(ξ),Qν​(1−ξ)), and the maximum by the comonotonic coupling (Qμ​(ξ),Qν​(ξ)), where ξ∼Unif(0,1).
Theorem 2.3 provides a closed-form characterization of the optimal value of 1D OT problems. We will leverage this characterization to derive tight bounds for PRTEs later.

2.3 Notation

We use P and E for probability and expectation, and ⊥⊥ for (conditional) independence. 1(⋅) denotes the indicator function. We write d for the differential or Lebesgue measure. For a probability measure μ on R, Qμ​(t) denotes its quantile function. Π(μ,ν) denotes the set of all couplings of two probability measures μ and ν, and W1​(μ,ν)=∫01​∣Qμ​(t)−Qν​(t)∣dt their 1-Wasserstein distance. Calligraphic letters X,Y,Z,W denote domains of the corresponding variables. We write OP​(⋅) and oP​(⋅) for stochastic order notation: Xn​=OP​(an​) means Xn​/an​ is bounded in probability, and Xn​=oP​(an​) means Xn​/an​P​0. A table collecting the variables and symbols used throughout the paper is given in O1 of the Online Appendix.

3 Partial Identification via Optimal Transport

3.1 CCOT Formulation of Partial Identification

In this section, we demonstrate how to derive tight, closed-form bounds for the PRTE. We begin by formally mapping the partial identification problem into an optimal transport framework.
The core intuition is to search over all possible joint distributions of the latent and observable variables (Y(0),Y(1),U,X,Z,W) that are compatible with both the observed data and the structural conditions in Assumption 2.1. Because the potential outcomes are conditionally independent of the instrument given X, the identifying power of our model is entirely captured by the joint distributions of (Y(w),U,X) for w∈{0,1}.
Let πw​ denote the joint probability measure of (Y(w),U,X) and let πw​(⋅∣x,u) denote the conditional distribution of Y(w) given x,u. Recall that our target parameter is a linear functional of these measures:
θω​(π0​,π1​)=E(X,U,Y(1))∼π1​​[Y(1)ω(X,U)]−E(X,U,Y(0))∼π0​​[Y(0)ω(X,U)].
To achieve sharp bounds, we must constrain πw​ using all available observational information. Let Pobs​ denote the true observed joint distribution of (Y,W,Z,X). Under the threshold-crossing model in Assumption 2.1, while U is generally unobserved, its conditional distribution is explicitly tied to the treatment status and the propensity score. Specifically, conditional on X and Z, the event W=1 perfectly corresponds to U⩽p(Z,X), and W=0 corresponds to U>p(Z,X).
Together with the observed distribution of (X,Z), the joint distributions π0​ and π1​ fully determine the observational distribution of (X,Z,W,Y). To see this, we can link the unknown structural distributions directly to the observed conditional distribution of the data by exploiting the consistency equation Y=WY(1)+(1−W)Y(0) and the selection mechanism W=1(U⩽p(Z,X)). For any measurable set A⊆Y, the following identity holds for PZ,X​-almost every (z,x):
Pobs​(Y∈A,W=1∣Z=z,X=x)​=P(Y(1)∈A,U⩽p(z,x)∣Z=z,X=x).​
By the conditional independence assumption Z⊥⊥(Y(1),U)∣X, we can omit Z in the second conditioning:
P(Y(1)∈A,U⩽p(z,x)∣Z=z,X=x)​=P(Y(1)∈A,U⩽p(z,x)∣X=x).​
Since instruments that generate the same propensity value p(z,x) yield the same right-hand side conditional on X=x, we can replace conditioning on the full instrument value Z=z with conditioning on the scalar propensity value p(Z,X)=p(z,x) together with X=x. Next, we disintegrate the joint measures πw​ into the conditional distribution of the potential outcome given the covariates and the latent variable. The threshold-crossing rule selects U⩽p(z,x) into treatment and U>p(z,x) out of it, so write R1​(p):=(0,p] and R0​(p):=(p,1] for the two selected regions. Because U∣X∼Unif(0,1), integrating over Rw​(p) yields, for P∣X=x-almost every p and each w∈{0,1},
Pobs​(Y∈A,W=w∣p(Z,X)=p,X=x)​=∫Rw​(p)​πw​(A∣u,x)du.​
Write P=p(Z,X). Because a regular conditional law at an exact value of a continuous propensity score is defined only almost surely, first define, for P∣X=x-almost every p, the observed finite-measure-valued maps
Hw,x​(p,dy):=Pobs​(Y∈dy,W=w∣P=p,X=x),w∈{0,1}.(3.1)
To select canonical versions at every point of the conditional propensity support, let Kw,x​(dy∣u) be a regular conditional law of Y(w) given (U,X)=(u,x). Under Assumption 2.1, the preceding derivation gives
Hw,x​(p,dy)=∫Rw​(p)​Kw,x​(dy∣u)du,w∈{0,1},
for P∣X=x-almost every p. The right-hand sides are Lipschitz in total variation and hence extend the observed equivalence classes in (3.1) continuously to supp(P∣X=x). This extension is unique: two continuous versions that agree almost surely under the conditional law of P agree everywhere on its support. We henceforth use Hw,x​ for these canonical observed versions. Thus Hw,x​ is identified from Pobs​ on the conditional propensity support, including its endpoints even when the corresponding singleton events have probability zero; the latent kernels Kw,x​ themselves need not be identified. With no covariates we write Hw​. Furthermore, by construction, the marginal distribution of (U,X) under πw​ must equal the known population distribution PU,X​.
This allows us to formulate the partial identification of the PRTE as the following infinite-dimensional linear programming problem, in which every constraint is imposed for both w∈{0,1}:
π0​,π1​max​ /π0​,π1​min​subject to​θω​(π0​,π1​)∫Rw​(p(z,x))​πw​(dy∣u,x)du=Hw,x​(p(z,x),dy),PZ,X​-a.e. (z,x),πw​(dx,du)=du Pobs​(dx),πw​ is supported on Y×[0,1]×X.​(3.2)
We call the optimization in (3.2) the Constrained Conditional Optimal Transport (CCOT) problem. The feasible set is constrained by the observational compatibility conditions in (3.2); the problem is conditional in that, for fixed covariates x and latent resistance u, it seeks a conditional measure πw​(⋅∣u,x) on Y; and it is a transport problem because the objective is linear in πw​(⋅∣u,x) with effective cost c(y,u,x)=y⋅ω(x,u), so that mass is transported from the latent space U to the outcome space Y(w) conditional on X.
To formally guarantee that the CCOT formulation in (3.2) yields sharp bounds for the PRTE, we must show that any pair of measures (π0​,π1​) satisfying the CCOT constraints corresponds to a valid data-generating process that satisfies our structural assumptions and perfectly reproduces the observed data. Let Γ(Pobs​) be the set of all measure pairs (π0​,π1​) satisfying the constraints in (3.2). The following proposition characterizes the joint distribution of (Y(0),Y(1),U,X), from which observational equivalence of the marginal pair (π0​,π1​) follows immediately.
Proposition 3.1 (Sharp Identified Set of the Joint Latent Law).
Suppose the observed distribution Pobs​ is generated by a true structural model satisfying Assumption 2.1. Let π~ be any probability measure on Y×Y×[0,1]×X whose (Y(w),U,X)-marginals π~w​ satisfy (π~0​,π~1​)∈Γ(Pobs​). Then there exists a joint distribution of the latent and observable variables (Y(0),Y(1),U,X,Z,W) such that:
  1. (i) the joint marginal distribution of (Y(0),Y(1),U,X) is exactly π~;
  2. (ii) Assumption 2.1 holds for (Y(0),Y(1),U,X,Z,W);
  3. (iii) the induced distribution of (Z,X,W,Y) exactly matches Pobs​.
Conversely, every joint marginal π~ arising from a distribution of (Y(0),Y(1),U,X,Z,W) satisfying (ii)–(iii) has (Y(w),U,X)-marginals in Γ(Pobs​) for w∈{0,1}.
The content of Proposition 3.1 is twofold. First, the CCOT constraints act only on the two marginals π~0​ and π~1​: any coupling of these marginals—including every joint law of (Y(0),Y(1)) given (U,X)—is observationally equivalent. Second, the converse makes the characterization sharp: no joint law outside this set can be generated by a structural model matching Pobs​. Consequently, the identified set for the PRTE target is {θω​(π0​,π1​):(π0​,π1​)∈Γ(Pobs​)}, and the maximum and minimum of θω​(π0​,π1​) over Γ(Pobs​) are the sharp upper and lower bounds on the PRTE. The proof is given in A.
Remark 3.2.
The fact that the moment relaxation approach of Mogstad et~al. (2018) can yield arbitrarily loose bounds compared to our CCOT formulation is well-recognized; see also Han and Yang (2024). A detailed comparison example is given in Example O2.2 of the Online Appendix.
Remark 3.3 (Beyond PRTE: CCOT for general joint functionals).
The CCOT perspective is not specific to the PRTE. At a conceptual level, one could consider a bounded measurable cost f:Y2→R and the joint target θf​:=E[f(Y(1),Y(0))] by replacing the PRTE objective in (3.2) with Eπ​[f(Y(1),Y(0))] and enlarging the decision variable from the pair (π0​,π1​) to a joint conditional kernel π(dy1​,dy0​∣u,x) whose marginals satisfy the same observational constraints. A sharp characterization should again follow from the lifting logic behind Proposition 3.1. What is special about the PRTE is the separable product cost y⋅ω(x,u): it allows the CCOT problem to collapse into one-dimensional OT problems for each potential outcome separately. For a general joint functional, that separability is lost, and the resulting interval-specific problems are instead OT problems over the coupling between the identified marginals of Y(1) and Y(0), with no comparable closed-form reduction in general. Since the present paper is about the PRTE case, we do not pursue this extension here.
Next, we show how to obtain a closed-form solution to the CCOT problem (3.2). Notice that in (3.2), the objective is the difference of two linear functionals of π0​ and π1​, and the constraints on π0​ and π1​ are separate. Therefore, we only need to consider one side of the problem, as the other side follows identically. In what follows, we only consider the W=1 side minimization problem, i.e.,
π1​min​subject to​Eπ1​​[Y(1)ω(X,U)]∫0p(z,x)​π1​(dy∣u,x)du=H1,x​(p(z,x),dy),PZ,X​-a.e. (z,x)π1​(dx,du)=du Pobs​(dx),π1​ is supported on Y×[0,1]×X.​(3.3)
The solution for the maximization problem can be derived similarly. Writing θω​=θω,1​−θω,0​, let [θ​ω,w​,θω,w​] denote the sharp identified interval for the w-th component. Because the feasible sets for π0​ and π1​ are Cartesian products, the sharp identified interval for the full target is
[θ​ω​,θω​]=[θ​ω,1​−θω,0​,θω,1​−θ​ω,0​].
Accordingly, we state the main derivations for θω,1​; the formulas for θω,0​ are obtained by the same arguments with the untreated analogues.

3.2 Closed-Form Bounds without Covariates

To better illustrate the idea, we first derive the results without covariates and generalize them in the next subsection. Therefore, in this subsection, ω and p do not depend on x.

3.2.1 Discrete Instrument Setting

We first consider the setting where there are no covariates and the instrument Z takes values in a finite discrete set Z. Let the unique positive values of the propensity score be ordered as
{p(z):z∈Z, p(z)>0}={p1​,…,pK​},
with the conventions p0​:=0 and pK+1​:=1, such that 0=p0​<p1​<p2​<⋯<pK​⩽pK+1​=1. Any instrument value with p(z)=0 is represented by the boundary level p0​ and contributes only the zero treated measure. We allow distinct instrument values to map to the same propensity value. This partitions the unit interval of the latent variable U into the K nonempty identified subintervals Ii​=(pi​,pi+1​], i=0,…,K−1, and the residual interval IK​=(pK​,1], which is empty when pK​=1.
Because the objective function (3.3) is an integral over U, it decomposes additively across these subintervals into one conditional-mean term per Ii​ plus a residual integral over (pK​,1]; the decomposed objective is displayed in (3.6) below.
The fundamental advantage of the discrete setting is that the global observational constraints can be differenced, perfectly isolating the conditional distribution of Y(1) within each interval Ii​. Recall that from (3.3),
∫0pi​​π1​(dy∣u)du=Pobs​(dy,W=1∣p(Z)=pi​),i=1,…,K.​​(3.4)​
The key step is a staircase reduction of the cumulative constraints in (3.4). Subtracting adjacent constraints converts the cumulative restrictions into interval-wise marginal restrictions, which in turn converts (3.3) into separate standard one-dimensional OT problems. For i=1,…,K−1, subtracting the i-th constraint from the (i+1)-th in (3.4) isolates the integral over (pi​,pi+1​]; for i=0, the first constraint directly governs (0,p1​]. Since cumulative sums recover the original constraints, this invertible transformation shows that the system (3.4) is equivalent to constraining the average of π1​(dy∣u) over each Ii​, i=0,…,K−1, to equal the identified measure
μ1,i​(dy)=⎩⎨⎧​p1​Pobs​(dy,W=1∣p(Z)=p1​)​,pi+1​−pi​Pobs​(dy,W=1∣p(Z)=pi+1​)−Pobs​(dy,W=1∣p(Z)=pi​)​,​if i=0,if 0<i<K.​​​(3.5)​
When the final interval IK​=(pK​,1] is nonempty, the potential outcome Y(1) is never observed there because no individual in the population has a propensity score high enough to induce treatment when U>pK​. By (3.4), since π1​ is nonnegative, Pobs​(dy,W=1∣p(Z)=p) is nondecreasing in p. Moreover, μ1,i​(Y)=1 since Pobs​(W=1∣p(Z)=p)=p. Therefore, the μ1,i​ are valid distributions. Mourifié and Wan (2017) provide a simple method to test the monotonicity of Pobs​(dy,W=1∣p(Z)=p).
For 0<i<K and any measurable set A, (3.5) gives
μ1,i​(A)​=pi+1​−pi​P(Y(1)∈A,U∈(0,pi+1​]∣p(Z)=pi+1​)−P(Y(1)∈A,U∈(0,pi​]∣p(Z)=pi​)​=P(Y(1)∈A∣U∈(pi​,pi+1​]),​
where we use Assumption 2.1(3) and consistency in the first equality and Assumption 2.1(2) in the second. Therefore, μ1,i​ can be interpreted as the distribution of the potential outcome under treatment for the i-th complier group. The i-th complier group consists of units with latent resistance U∈(pi​,pi+1​]: they refuse treatment at propensity values weakly below pi​ and take treatment once the propensity exceeds their latent threshold. In particular, when the instrument is binary, this recovers the identification results of Imbens and Rubin (1997).
Combining the additive decomposition of the objective with the interval-wise constraints just derived, the original problem (3.3) can be equivalently written as
π1​min​i=0∑K−1​(pi+1​−pi​)Eπ1​​[Y(1)ω(U)∣U∈Ii​]+∫pK​1​∫Y​yω(u)π1​(dy∣u)du(3.6)
subject to the K independent marginal constraints
​pi+1​−pi​1​∫pi​pi+1​​π1​(dy∣u)du=μ1,i​(dy),i=0,…,K−1,π1​(du)=du,​(3.7)
with the support constraint supp(π1​(⋅∣u))⊆Y for all u∈[0,1], and no further distributional constraint on π1​(⋅∣u) for u∈IK​=(pK​,1]. Crucially, each constraint in (3.7) involves π1​ only on the single interval Ii​, and the objective (3.6) is additively separable across these intervals. Therefore, the global problem decomposes into K constrained OT subproblems and one unconstrained residual problem, the latter contributing zero when pK​=1.
Specifically, for each interval i=0,…,K−1, the data pin down the marginal distribution of Y(1) as μ1,i​ and the marginal distribution of U as uniform on (pi​,pi+1​]. Let νi​ denote the uniform probability measure Unif(pi​,pi+1​). The set of valid joint distributions for (Y(1),U) conditional on U∈Ii​ is exactly the set of all couplings Π(μ1,i​,νi​). Therefore, for each of these K intervals, we solve a standard 1D optimal transport problem:
γi​∈Π(μ1,i​,νi​)min​∫Y×Ii​​y⋅ω(u)dγi​(y,u).(3.8)
By contrast, when the final interval IK​=(pK​,1] is nonempty, the propensity score never reaches a value high enough to induce treatment there, so the data impose no constraint whatsoever on the distribution of Y(1) for this subpopulation. Without distributional constraints, the optimal transport problem degenerates into a trivial pointwise minimization. Because ymin​ and ymax​ are the extrema of the compact outcome domain, for each u∈IK​ the optimal solution assigns all probability mass to ymin​ if ω(u)⩾0, or to ymax​ if ω(u)<0:
π1​min​∫pK​1​∫Y​yω(u)π1​(dy∣u)du = ∫pK​1​(ymin​max{0,ω(u)}+ymax​min{0,ω(u)})du.(3.9)
When pK​=1, this is an integral over the empty interval and equals zero. Summing the optimal values of the K constrained subproblems in (3.8) scaled by their respective interval lengths (pi+1​−pi​) and adding the trivial unconstrained bound from (3.9), we obtain the global minimum. Applying Theorem 2.3 to each subproblem in (3.8) yields the countermonotonic coupling, which leads directly to the following closed-form sharp bounds.
Theorem 3.4 (Closed-Form Sharp Bounds).
Suppose Assumption 2.1 and Assumption 2.2 hold, X is almost surely constant, and Z is finite. For i=0,…,K−1, let QY,i​(t) be the quantile function of the identified conditional distribution μ1,i​ defined in (3.5). Let Qω,i​(t) be the quantile function of the random variable ω(U) where U∼Unif(pi​,pi+1​). The sharp lower bound for the W=1 component of the PRTE is given by:
θ​ω,1​= ​i=0∑K−1​(pi+1​−pi​)∫01​QY,i​(t)Qω,i​(1−t)dt+∫pK​1​(ymin​max{0,ω(u)}+ymax​min{0,ω(u)})du.​(3.10)
Similarly, the sharp upper bound is given by replacing Qω,i​(1−t) with Qω,i​(t) in the OT term and swapping ymin​ and ymax​ in the trivial tail term.
We defer the formal proof of this theorem to that of Theorem 3.8 in A.2, since the present theorem is the constant-X special case with every LIV interval degenerate. Theorem 3.4 provides a closed-form, analytically tractable expression for the sharp bounds, bypassing any need for linear programming and requiring only estimation of the conditional quantile functions from the observed data.
As a special case, setting ω(u)=1 makes every Qω,i​≡1, so the OT term telescopes into the observed treated mean at pK​ and
θ​ω,1​=pK​E[Y∣W=1,p(Z)=pK​] + ymin​(1−pK​),
the classical bound of Manski (1990) for E[Y(1)], which is known to be tight [Heckman and Vytlacil, 2001]. 1 illustrates the three identification regions that compose the bound in Theorem 3.4; Example O2.1 of the Online Appendix works through a concrete binary-instrument example with a constant propensity score, deriving the explicit three-part decomposition.
By Theorem 3.4, the width of the identified interval is
θω,1​−θ​ω,1​​=i=0∑K−1​(pi+1​−pi​)∫01​(QY,i​(t)−QY,i​(1−t))Qω,i​(t)dt+(ymax​−ymin​)∫pK​1​∣ω(u)∣du,​
which depends on the range of the propensity function and on the distributions μ1,i​. If pK​ is close to 1 and the support of each μ1,i​ is small, the width is also small. In particular, if each QY,i​ is constant and pK​=1, then θω,1​ is point-identified from the data.
Remark 3.5 (Decomposition into 1D marginal constraints and Marx (2024)).
Marx (2024) raises the open question of characterizing the distribution of treatment effects for the complier group. Although Proposition 3.1 states sharpness at the joint level of (Y(0),Y(1),U,X), the CCOT constraints defining Γ(Pobs​) reduce to independent one-dimensional marginal constraints on the conditional kernels πw​(dy∣u,x), so once these marginals are pinned down the remaining freedom lies entirely in the coupling between Y(1) and Y(0) given (U,X). In the binary-instrument, no-covariate setting with p1​<p2​, the complier interval is Ic​=(p1​,p2​] and (3.5) identifies the treated-outcome distribution for compliers as μ1,1​; differencing the untreated component, which is nonincreasing in p, identifies
μ0,1​(dy):=p2​−p1​Pobs​(dy,W=0∣p(Z)=p1​)−Pobs​(dy,W=0∣p(Z)=p2​)​.
The identified set for the complier treatment-effect distribution is therefore exactly IΔ,c​={(y1​−y0​)#​γ:γ∈Π(μ1,1​,μ0,1​)}, so Marx's question becomes: once the identified complier marginals are fixed, characterize all pushforwards of their couplings under (y1​,y0​)↦y1​−y0​. Characterizing IΔ,c​ therefore reduces to determining the treatment-effect distributions generated by these couplings.

3.2.2 General Instrument Setting

We now consider a general instrument setting under a single regularity condition on the instrument domain and the propensity score. This framework nests the finite discrete case (each component a singleton), the connected continuous case studied in the local instrumental variables (LIV) literature [Heckman and Vytlacil, 1999], and mixtures of the two.
Assumption 3.6 (Finite-Component Propensity Continuity).
The instrument domain Z has finitely many connected components. For almost every x∈X, the conditional propensity score function z↦p(z,x)=P(W=1∣Z=z,X=x) is continuous on each connected component.
Under the standing compactness of Z and Assumption 3.6, the image of each connected component under p(⋅) is a closed interval (possibly a singleton if p is constant on the component or if the component is a single point). Merging overlaps and ordering from left to right, the range of the propensity score admits a maximal-interval decomposition
p(Z)=k=1⋃K​[p​k​,p​k​],0⩽p​1​⩽p​1​<p​2​⩽p​2​<⋯<p​K​⩽p​K​⩽1,(3.11)
where we explicitly allow degenerate intervals p​k​=p​k​ corresponding to isolated propensity values, as in the finite discrete case. Adopting the boundary conventions p​0​:=0 and p​K+1​:=1, this decomposition partitions the unit interval of the latent variable U into three types of regions: the LIV intervals Lk​:=[p​k​,p​k​] for k=1,…,K, the OT gaps Gk​:=(p​k​,p​k+1​) for k=0,…,K−1, and the trivial tail (p​K​,1].
The CCOT problem for the treated (W=1) component becomes
π1​min​subject to​Eπ1​​[Y(1)ω(U)]∫0p​π1​(dy∣u)du=H1​(p,dy), ∀p∈p(Z),π1​(du)=du.​(3.12)
Following the same strategy as in 3.2.1, we rewrite (3.12) into a manifestly separable form across the three region types. The objective splits additively as
Eπ1​​[Y(1)ω(U)]​=k=0∑K−1​∫Gk​​∫Y​yω(u)π1​(dy∣u)du+k=1∑K​∫Lk​​∫Y​yω(u)π1​(dy∣u)du+∫p​K​1​∫Y​yω(u)π1​(dy∣u)du.​
On each gap Gk​, the same telescoping argument that produced (3.5)—differencing the observational constraint in (3.12) at p=p​k​ and p=p​k+1​—fixes the marginal of Y(1) on Gk​ to be
μ1,k​(dy):=p​k+1​−p​k​H1​(p​k+1​,dy)−H1​(p​k​,dy)​,k: p​k​<p​k+1​,(3.13)
where H1​(0,⋅)=0 by definition. Thus the k=0 formula applies when p​1​>0; when p​1​=0, G0​ is empty and has zero contribution. More generally, empty gaps are omitted from all gap-specific definitions and sums below. Let g1c​(p):=∫Y​yH1​(p,dy), and fix the countable measure-determining class A:={Y∩(−∞,r]:r∈Q}∪{Y}. On each non-degenerate LIV interval Lk​, the constraint in (3.12) holds for every p∈[p​k​,p​k​]. For each A∈A, the scalar map p↦H1​(p,A) is absolutely continuous on Lk​ and the ordinary fundamental theorem of calculus gives
π1​(A∣u)=∂p∂​​p=u​H1​(p,A),A∈A,u∈Lk​ a.e.(3.14)
Countability of A gives one common null set, so (3.14) identifies π1​(⋅∣u) almost everywhere on Lk​. Applying the same scalar argument to the bounded function y gives ∂u​g1c​(u)=∫Y​yπ1​(dy∣u) almost everywhere. The trivial tail (p​K​,1] carries no constraint. Because cumulative sums of the gap marginals plus integration of the identified LIV kernels recover the original constraint at every p∈p(Z), this transformation is invertible and the two constraint systems are equivalent. Each rewritten constraint involves π1​ only on its own region and the objective is additively separable, so the global problem decomposes into three types of subproblems, one for each region type.
  1. The OT gaps Gk​, k=0,…,K−1: the Y(1)-marginal is fixed to μ1,k​ of (3.13) and the U-marginal is Unif(Gk​), so the contribution of Gk​ is a standard 1D OT problem, solved by Theorem 2.3. Empty gaps contribute zero.
  2. The LIV intervals Lk​, k=1,…,K: for non-degenerate Lk​, the LIV identity (3.14) point-identifies E[Y(1)∣U=u]=∂u​g1c​(u) for a.e. u∈Lk​, so the contribution is uniquely determined. Degenerate Lk​ contribute a Lebesgue-null integral and drop out.

Combining the solutions across these regions yields the closed-form sharp bounds for the general instrument setting, which are illustrated in 6 of the Appendix.
Theorem 3.7 (General Closed-Form Sharp Bounds).
Suppose Assumption 2.1, Assumption 2.2, and Assumption 3.6 hold, and X is almost surely constant. Let p(Z)=⋃k=1K​[p​k​,p​k​] be the maximal-interval decomposition in (3.11). The proof combines the subtraction-of-constraints decomposition from Theorem 3.4 (applied region-by-region to identify μ1,k​ on each gap) with the LIV-derivative argument on each non-degenerate interval Lk​, followed by the 1D OT coupling of Theorem 2.3. 3.3 Closed-Form Bounds with Covariates

Generalizing the previous results to covariates is mathematically straightforward. Because Assumption 2.1 imposes Z⊥⊥(Y(w),U)∣X, the global CCOT problem disintegrates into a family of conditional one-dimensional optimal transport problems indexed by x∈X: we solve conditional on X=x and aggregate the conditional bounds over the marginal distribution of X by iterated expectations.
Under Assumption 3.6, for Pobs​-a.e. x∈X, the conditional range of the propensity score admits a maximal-interval decomposition
p(Z,x)=k=1⋃Kx​​[p​k​(x),p​k​(x)],0⩽p​1​(x)⩽p​1​(x)<⋯<p​Kx​​(x)⩽p​Kx​​(x)⩽1,(3.16)
with degenerate intervals p​k​(x)=p​k​(x) corresponding to isolated conditional propensity values and boundary conventions p​0​(x):=0 and p​Kx​+1​(x):=1. For each x, this partitions [0,1] into the conditional LIV intervals Lk​(x):=[p​k​(x),p​k​(x)], the OT gaps Gk​(x):=(p​k​(x),p​k+1​(x)), and the trivial tail (p​Kx​​(x),1]. The conditional gap-identified measure of Y(1) on Gk​(x) is
μ1,k∣x​(dy):=p​k+1​(x)−p​k​(x)H1,x​(p​k+1​(x),dy)−H1,x​(p​k​(x),dy)​,(3.17)
for indices k such that p​k​(x)<p​k+1​(x); H1,x​(0,⋅)=0 by definition. Empty conditional gaps are omitted and contribute zero. Finally, let g1c​(p,x):=∫Y​yH1,x​(p,dy). This canonical version is absolutely continuous in p on each non-degenerate LIV interval Lk​(x), and every derivative below means its intervalwise Lebesgue-a.e. derivative.
Theorem 3.8 (Conditional General Bound).
Suppose Assumption 2.1, Assumption 2.2, and Assumption 3.6 hold. For each nonempty conditional gap Gk​(x), let QY,k∣x​(t) be the quantile function of μ1,k∣x​ defined in (3.17), and Qω,k∣x​(t) the quantile function of ω(x,U) for U∼Unif(Gk​(x)). In the displayed sums, a term indexed by an empty conditional gap is defined to be zero. The sharp lower bound for the W=1 component of the target parameter is
θ​ω,1​=EX​[​k=0∑KX​−1​(p​k+1​(X)−p​k​(X))∫01​QY,k∣X​(t)Qω,k∣X​(1−t)dt+k=1∑KX​​∫p​k​(X)p​k​(X)​dud​g1c​(u,X)ω(X,u)du+∫p​KX​​(X)1​(ymin​max{0,ω(X,u)}+ymax​min{0,ω(X,u)})du].​(3.18)
Similarly, the sharp upper bound is given by replacing Qω,k∣X​(1−t) with Qω,k∣X​(t) in the OT term and swapping ymin​ and ymax​ in the trivial tail term.
The proof of Theorem 3.8 is given in A.2. The two limit cases stated after Theorem 3.7 carry over verbatim under x-conditioning: degenerate conditional LIV intervals reduce (3.18) to the discrete covariate bound, and KX​=1 with p​1​(X)<p​1​(X) recovers the standard LIV covariate bound.

4 Estimation and Inference

In this section, we develop estimation and inference results for the closed-form bounds derived in 3. For the discrete instrument setting, we leverage DML [Chernozhukov et~al., 2018] to accommodate high-dimensional covariates, constructing Neyman-orthogonal scores that yield n​-consistent and asymptotically normal estimators. In the continuous instrument setting, we characterize the corresponding nonparametric convergence rates. Throughout, we observe an i.i.d. sample {Oi​}i=1n​ of O=(X,Z,W,Y)∼Pobs​, and η collects the nuisance functions entering the bound, with η^​ its estimate.
We model the alternative policy as q(z,x)=ϕ(z,x,p(z,x)), where the known map ϕ:Z×X×[0,1]→[0,1] is jointly measurable. Common examples include propensity shifts ϕ(z,x,p)=p+α or p(1+α) on designs for which the shifted propensities remain in [0,1], or setting ϕ(z,x,p)=r(z,x) to evaluate a specific alternative policy r.
We focus our exposition on the bounds for the PRTE because the derivations for other causal quantities proceed similarly. For simplicity, we first develop theory for the unscaled numerator E[Yq−Y]. In the empirical designs considered below, the PRTE denominator is the known policy-shift size α>0, so the reported bounds and confidence intervals for PRTEα​ are obtained by dividing the corresponding numerator bounds by α. More generally, when E[q(Z,X)−p(Z,X)] is not fixed by design, it is point-identified and can be estimated separately. Thus, our target weight function simplifies to
ω(x,u)≡Eobs​[1(u⩽q(Z,X))−1(u⩽p(Z,X))∣X=x].​

4.1 Discrete Instrument Setting

For a fixed x, the weight function ω(x,u) is a step function that is non-increasing on each latent interval u∈(pi​(x),pi+1​(x)], with jumps only at the alternative-policy values q(z,x) falling inside that interval. This piecewise structure allows us to decompose the closed-form lower bound integral into a finite weighted sum over the instrument level sets.
Define qj,i​(x) as the j-th smallest value of the alternative policy propensity q(z,x) that falls in the baseline bin [pi​(x),pi+1​(x)) for i<K and in the closed final bin [pK​(x),1] for i=K, ordered as follows:
pi​(x)⩽q1,i​(x)<⋯<qli​,i​(x)<pi+1​(x)(i<K),
with the boundary conventions q0,i​(x)=pi​(x) and qli​+1,i​(x)=pi+1​(x). Let the baseline and alternative instrument level sets be
Sk​={z∈Z:p(z,x)=pk​(x)},Tj,k​={z∈Z:q(z,x)=qj,k​(x)},j=1,…,lk​.​
For the final bin, the last displayed strict inequality is replaced by qlK​,K​(x)⩽pK+1​(x)=1. Here q0,i​ and qli​+1,i​ are integration boundaries; set T0,i​=Tli​+1,i​=∅. Thus, if q1,i​=pi​, instruments attaining that value belong only to T1,i​, while an alternative propensity equal to one belongs to TlK​,K​ and is retained in the tail term. Values of u exactly on a boundary are Lebesgue-null and do not affect the target integral.
The DML scores developed after the reduction differentiate q(z,x)=ϕ(z,x,p(z,x)) with respect to the propensity score, so we impose the following condition only for inference.
Assumption 4.1 (Policy-Map Smoothness).
The map ϕ(z,x,p) is differentiable with respect to p, and ∂p∂ϕ​ is bounded and uniformly Lipschitz in p for all z∈Z and x∈X.
This condition controls the pathwise derivative and its second-order remainder.
We impose the following separation condition to consistently estimate the level sets.
Assumption 4.2 (Propensity-Level Separation).
  1. There exists a constant cgap​>0 such that, for all x∈X and all v,v′∈Rx​={p(z,x),q(z,x)}z∈Z​, either v′=v or ∣v−v′∣>cgap​. Moreover, the equality classes and their strict ordering are invariant in x: the sets Sk​, Tj,k​ and their indices K,lk​ do not depend on x.
  2. For every k=0,…,K−1 and every nonempty Tj,k​, qj,k​(x)=pk​(x) for all x. Under part (i), this implies qj,k​(x)>pk​(x)+cgap​ for k⩾1.
Part (i) implies the stable level sets needed by the finite-dimensional reduction and the clustering step below. We therefore suppress the dependence on x in Sk​, Tj,k​, K, and lk​ from now on. Part (ii) keeps a nonempty pooled policy boundary distinct from the structural boundary q0,k​=pk​ in the displayed continuous-outcome quantile score and binary active-set score. We impose this condition only to simplify the clustering labels and score formulas; it is not required for identification. It can be removed by using a more elaborate clustering method that detects the coinciding boundaries.
Because Z is finite, Assumption 3.6 holds trivially and every conditional LIV interval in Theorem 3.8 is degenerate, so that theorem specializes to the covariate version of Theorem 3.4; we refer to it in this form throughout the subsection. The resulting bound admits a representation as an expectation of a finite weighted sum over instrument level sets and their sub-intervals. Before stating this representation, we introduce the nuisance components that carry the observable content of the bound.
Nuisance components. The representation below is assembled from five objects, defined for each interval index k∈{0,…,K} and sub-interval index j∈{0,…,lk​}. The first two are the aggregate weights that the step weight ω assigns to instruments,
γfull,k​(x)γj,k​(x)​:=Pobs​(Z∈i=k+1⋃K​l=0⋃li​​Tl,i​​X=x)−Pobs​(Z∈i=k+1⋃K​Si​​X=x),:=Pobs​​Z∈l=j⋃lk​​Tl,k​​X=x​,​
where γfull,k​∈[−1,1] because it differences two conditional probabilities. The next two carry the outcome distribution: with the relative threshold κj,k​(x):=(qj,k​(x)−pk​(x))/(pk+1​(x)−pk​(x))∈[0,1],
Jfull,k​(x)Jj,k​(x)​:=(pk+1​(x)−pk​(x))Eμ1,k∣x​​[Y],:=(pk+1​(x)−pk​(x))∫κj,k​(x)κj+1,k​(x)​QY,k∣x​(u)du,​
where μ1,k∣x​ is the identified conditional complier distribution of (3.17) and QY,k∣x​ is its quantile function. The fifth is the trivial-bound boundary term
ΔK​(x):=ymin​Eobs​[1(Z∈j=1⋃lK​​Tj,K​)(q(Z,X)−pK​(X))​X=x].
This is the tail term of Theorem 3.8 under the PRTE weight: since p(z,x)⩽pK​(x) for every z, the weight satisfies ω(x,u)=Eobs​[1(u⩽q(Z,X))∣X=x]⩾0 on (pK​(x),1], so the ymax​ branch of the tail integral is inactive, and Fubini converts ymin​∫pK​(x)1​ω(x,u)du into the displayed expectation.
Estimating these five requires three further level-set quantities that do not appear in the representation itself—the tail weight γK​(x):=Pobs​(Z∈⋃j=1lK​​Tj,K​∣X=x), the within-set assignment shares aj,k​(z,x):=Pobs​(Z=z∣Z∈Tj,k​,X=x), and the pooled representation qj,k​(x)=∑z∈Tj,k​​aj,k​(z,x)q(z,x) that extends the policy level regularly when estimated instrument-specific levels are not exactly tied. The latter two are detailed in B.1, and all three enter only through the scores.
Proposition 4.3 (Discrete-Instrument Reduction to Nuisance Functional).
Suppose Assumption 2.1 and part (i) of Assumption 4.2 hold and Z is finite. Then the sharp lower bound in Theorem 3.8 admits the representation
θ​ω,1​=E[k=0∑K−1​(γfull,k​(X)Jfull,k​(X)+j=1∑lk​​γj,k​(X)Jj−1,k​(X))+ΔK​(X)].​​(4.1)​
The sharp upper bound admits an analogous representation, obtained by replacing QY,k∣x​(u) by QY,k∣x​(1−u) inside Jj,k​ and swapping ymin​ with ymax​ in ΔK​.
Proposition 4.3 is the key analytical step that converts the optimal-transport integral in Theorem 3.8 into a Neyman-orthogonalizable functional of standard nuisance quantities—conditional probabilities, conditional means, and conditional quantile integrals. The proof, given in O3.1 of the Online Appendix, exploits the piecewise-constant, monotone structure of ω(X,⋅) on each baseline interval and identifies the step-function value attached to each sub-interval (qj,k​(X),qj+1,k​(X)).
The sub-interval term Jj,k​ still involves the conditional quantile function QY,k∣X​, which is delicate to estimate directly. The next proposition replaces it with conditional expectations in the two outcome regimes of interest.
Proposition 4.4 (Specialization of the Sub-Interval Contribution).
Fix k∈{0,…,K−1}. Set the lower boundary ν0,k​(x)≡ymin​, and let νj,k​(x):=QY,k∣x​(κj,k​(x)) for j∈{1,…,lk​}.
  1. Continuous outcome. If μ1,k∣X​ is continuous at νj,k​(X) and νj+1,k​(X) almost surely, then, for j∈{0,…,lk​−1},
    Jj,k​(X)=(pk+1​(X)−pk​(X))Eμ1,k∣X​​[Y1(νj,k​(X)<Y⩽νj+1,k​(X))].(4.2)
  2. Binary outcome. If Y∈{0,1}, then Jfull,k​(X)=P1,k+1​(X)−P1,k​(X) with P1,k​(x):=Eobs​[YW∣Z∈Sk​,X=x] for k⩾1 and the boundary convention P1,0​(x)≡0, and for j∈{1,…,lk​},
    Jj−1,k​(X)=hj,k−​(X):=max(0,qj,k​(X)−max(qj−1,k​(X),pk+1​(X)−Jfull,k​(X))).(4.3)
    Consequently, (4.1) collapses to
    θ​ω,1​=E[k=0∑K−1​(γfull,k​(X)Jfull,k​(X)+j=1∑lk​​γj,k​(X)hj,k−​(X))+ΔK​(X)].​​(4.4)​
Part (i) converts the sub-interval quantile integral into a plain conditional expectation of Y on the quantile-defined band (νj,k​,νj+1,k​], so only the lk​+1 boundary quantiles νj,k​—rather than the full quantile process—enter the estimation. Part (ii) leverages the step-function form of QY,k∣X​ when Y is binary: the complier mean Eμ1,k∣X​​[Y] reduces to a difference of observed joint probabilities, and the integral of the step function over [κj−1,k​,κj,k​] evaluates to the closed-form hj,k−​. Both parts are proved in O3.2 of the Online Appendix.
Together, Proposition 4.3, Proposition 4.4 expose (4.1) as a functional of conditional expectations, boundary quantiles, and instrument-level-set probabilities—the form required for DML-style n​-inference. In both outcome regimes the estimator takes the same aggregated Neyman-orthogonal form,
θ​^​ω,1​=∣I2​∣1​i∈I2​∑​[k=0∑K−1​(ψ^​full,kprod​(Oi​;η^​)+j=1∑lk​​ψ^​j,kprod​(Oi​;η^​))+ψ^​ΔK​​(Oi​;η^​)],(4.5)
where each ψ^​ is a Neyman-orthogonal score that corrects for the estimation error of its associated nuisance. What differs across the two regimes is the nuisance list η^​, and hence the score formulas: these are given in C.1 for a continuous outcome and in C.2 for a discrete one. We treat the two regimes in turn and then state a single asymptotic normality result covering both.

4.1.1 Continuous Outcome

We first treat the case where the conditional complier distribution μ1,k∣X​ is continuous at the boundary quantiles νj,k​(X), so Proposition 4.4(i) applies. Recall that νj,k​(x)=QY,k∣x​(κj,k​(x)) denotes the boundary quantile introduced in Proposition 4.4. The representation (4.2) converts each sub-interval term Jj,k​(X) into a conditional expectation over the band (νj,k​(X),νj+1,k​(X)], thereby reducing the nuisance list from the full quantile process to the boundary quantiles νj,k​ alone. The Neyman-orthogonal score construction additionally requires the conditional indicator expectations
Mj,k+​(x)Mj,k−​(x)​:=E[1(Y⩽νj,k​(x))∣Z∈Sk+1​,W=1,X=x],:=E[1(Y⩽νj,k​(x))∣Z∈Sk​,W=1,X=x],​
which enter the Riesz representers αpk​​,αpk+1​​ for the pathwise derivatives with respect to the interval boundaries pk​,pk+1​, and whose own estimation error is corrected by the residuals IFMj,k±​​ (see C.1).
The functional form in (4.1) and (4.2) fixes the nuisance list η^​ entering (4.5); the rest of this subsection develops the corresponding estimators, trained on an auxiliary sample I1​.
Estimation Procedure. Following the standard DML template, we randomly partition the sample into an auxiliary set I1​ and a main estimation set I2​. On I1​ we estimate the propensity score p, clip it to [0,1], and set q^​=ϕ(⋅,⋅,p^​); using only the covariates in I2​, we average p^​ and q^​ over X and recover the level sets Sk​ and Tj,k​ as connected components of the graph that joins two averaged values lying within cgap​/2 of each other. Given those sets we fit the remaining nuisances on I1​—the interval boundaries p^​k​, the probability weights γ^​, π^k​, τ^j,k​ and within-set shares a^j,k​, the boundary quantiles ν^j,k​, and the conditional expectations M^j,k±​, J^j,k±​, J^full,k±​—clipping each to its known range, and finally average the plug-in orthogonal scores over I2​ to form (4.5). 1 states the procedure step by step; the explicit graph construction, the moment equation defining νj,k​, the conditional-expectation components, and the Neyman-orthogonal scores ψprod are given in B.1 and C.1.
Let πk​(x):=Pobs​(Z∈Sk​∣X=x) and τj,k​(x):=Pobs​(Z∈Tj,k​∣X=x) denote the conditional probabilities of the baseline and alternative-policy level sets. The following overlap assumption bounds the inverse probability weights in the debiased terms.
Assumption 4.5 (Overlap).
There exists a constant cπ​>0 such that πk​(x)⩾cπ​ for every x∈X and observed positive-propensity level k∈{1,…,K}, and τj,k​(x)⩾cπ​ for every nonempty alternative-policy level set Tj,k​.
The index k=0 is the structural convention p0​≡0 and need not correspond to a nonempty instrument level set. Accordingly, every minus-side conditional expectation, inverse-probability correction, and propensity residual indexed by k=0 is omitted from the scores; it is multiplied by the known boundary mass p0​=0.

4.1.2 Discrete Outcome

When the outcome Y takes finitely many values—in particular, when Y∈{0,1} is binary—the conditional quantile function QY,k∣X​ becomes a step function with atoms, and the continuity hypothesis of Proposition 4.4(i) fails. Instead, Proposition 4.4(ii) applies: the representation (4.4) expresses Jfull,k​ as a difference of observed joint probabilities P1,k+1​−P1,k​ and evaluates the sub-interval contribution in closed form through hj,k−​, so the nuisance list collapses to conditional expectations alone and quantile estimation is avoided entirely. We present the binary case; the extension to general discrete outcomes is analogous.
The estimator is again (4.5), now with the scores of C.2. The nuisance-estimation procedure mirrors 1 with the conditional-quantile and indicator-expectation steps removed, and with one addition: because the P^1,k​ are fitted on different instrument subsets, they need not be monotone in k in finite samples, so they are clipped to [0,1] and rearranged before J^full,k​=P^1,k+1∗​−P^1,k∗​ is formed. 2 states the procedure and B.2 and C.2 give the full details and the orthogonal scores.
To ensure differentiability of the target functional with respect to the nuisance parameters, we impose the following gap condition, which replaces the conditional-density smoothness required by part (i) of Theorem 4.7.
Assumption 4.6 (Lower-Boundary Discrete Outcome Gap).
There exists ch​>0 such that, for every k=0,…,K−1 with lk​⩾1 and j=0,…,lk​, almost surely,
∣pk+1​(X)−Jfull,k​(X)−qj,k​(X)∣⩾ch​.
This separation makes branch-selection errors for the lower bound second order under the stated L2​ rates, including at the fixed lower boundary q0,k​=pk​. It guarantees that the lower target is pathwise-differentiable in the nuisances despite the max operators appearing in hj,k−​. The symmetric upper estimator, when used, requires the analogous separation ∣pk​+Jfull,k​−qj,k​∣⩾ch​ for j=1,…,lk​+1.

4.1.3 Asymptotic Normality

The two regimes share a common set of conditions—the structural assumptions, the level-set separation and overlap conditions, and n−1/4 nuisance rates with clipping—and differ only in what is required at the sub-interval boundaries: a conditional density near each boundary quantile when the outcome is continuous, and the gap condition Assumption 4.6 when it is discrete. A single theorem therefore covers both; both parts are proved in D.
Theorem 4.7 (Asymptotic Normality).
Suppose Assumption 2.1, Assumption 4.1, Assumption 4.2, and Assumption 4.5 hold and Z is finite. Suppose the pre-recovery first stage fitted on I1​ satisfies maxz∈Z​∥p^​(z,⋅)−p(z,⋅)∥L2​​=oP​(n−1/4). Given the recovered level sets, suppose the remaining score nuisances fitted on I1​ are clipped to their known bounded ranges, every estimated conditional probability is clipped to [0,1] before any difference is formed, π^k​ and τ^j,k​ are clipped further to [cπ​/2,1], and the estimators converge componentwise at rate oP​(n−1/4) in L2​. Suppose in addition that one of the following holds.
  1. Continuous outcome. The nuisances include the boundary quantiles νj,k​, and, uniformly in X, each relevant conditional law Y∣X,Z∈Sk′​,W=1 has a density bounded in a fixed neighborhood of every true boundary νj,k​(X), j=1,…,lk​, for k′=k+1 and also for k′=k when k⩾1; at the fixed boundary ν0,k​=ymin​, these conditional laws have no atom at ymin​.
  2. Discrete outcome. The outcome is binary, Assumption 4.6 holds, and the nuisances are pk​, P1,k​, πk​, τj,k​, aj,k​, γfull,k​, γj,k​, and γK​.
Then the sample-split estimator (4.5) is n​-consistent and asymptotically normal:
n/2​(θ​^​ω,1​−θ​ω,1​)d​N(0,σ2),
where the asymptotic variance is the variance of the true orthogonal score, σ2=E[(ψ(O;η)−θ​ω,1​)2]. It can be consistently estimated by its sample analog σ^2=∣I2​∣1​∑i∈I2​​(ψ^​(Oi​;η^​)−θ​^​ω,1​)2.

4.2 Continuous Instrument Setting

We now consider a connected instrument domain Z. Write P=p(Z,X) and define
p​(x):=z∈Zinf​p(z,x),p​(x):=z∈Zsup​p(z,x),qtr(z,x):=min{p​(x),max{p​(x),q(z,x)}}.​
The standing compactness of Z and continuity of z↦p(z,x) imply that the conditional support of P is the interval [p​(x),p​(x)]. Define g1​(u,x):=g1c​(u,x)=∫Y​yH1,x​(u,dy), the canonical absolutely continuous version of Eobs​[YW∣P=u,X=x]. The truncated policy propensity qtr is needed because this function is identified only on the conditional support. For p​(x)>0, let
μ1,p​∣x​(dy):=p​(x)H1,x​(p​(x),dy)​,(4.6)
and denote its quantile function by Q1,p​∣x​. Equivalently, it is the canonical boundary limit of L(Y∣W=1,P=p,X=x) as p↓p​(x) through the conditional support: it averages the law of Y(1) over 0<U⩽p​(x). When p​(x)=0, choose μ1,p​∣x​ arbitrarily; every expression below multiplies its contribution by p​(x) and is therefore invariant to this choice.
The general bound (3.18) contains the derivative ∂u​g1​(u,X). The next proposition integrates this derivative analytically, so the estimator never differentiates a nonparametric regression.
Proposition 4.8 (Continuous-Instrument Reduction via Fubini).
Suppose Assumption 2.1 and Assumption 3.6 hold, and Z is connected. Then the sharp lower bound in Theorem 3.8 admits the representation
θ​ω,1​​=EZ,X​[−∫min{p​(X),q(Z,X)}p​(X)​Q1,p​∣X​(v/p​(X))dv+g1​(qtr(Z,X),X)−g1​(P,X)+ymin​max{0,q(Z,X)−p​(X)}],​(4.7)
where the first integral is defined as zero when p​(X)=0. The sharp upper bound is obtained by replacing Q1,p​∣X​(v/p​(X)) with Q1,p​∣X​(1−v/p​(X)) and ymin​ with ymax​.
The first term uses the treated boundary law in (4.6); the second evaluates g1​ only at P and at the support projection qtr(Z,X). This lower truncation matters for policies with q(Z,X)<p​(X): the movement below p​(X) belongs to the OT gap term, whereas the LIV contribution stops at p​(X). The third term covers q(Z,X)>p​(X). The proof is given in O3.3 of the Online Appendix.
Proposition 4.8 motivates a plug-in estimator, obtained by replacing each nuisance in (4.7) with a machine-learning estimate trained on auxiliary samples. We use three-way sample splitting with ∣Ij​∣/n→ρj​∈(0,1) for j=0,1,2: the sample I0​ estimates p, q, p​, and p​; conditional on I0​, the sample I1​ estimates g1​ and the treated boundary law; and I2​ evaluates the target. The estimator is
θ​^​ω,1​=∣I2​∣1​i∈I2​∑​(ψ^​1​(Oi​)+ψ^​2​(Oi​)+ψ^​3​(Oi​)),(4.8)
where ψ^​1​,ψ^​2​,ψ^​3​ substitute estimated nuisances into the three terms of (4.7). Throughout, P^=p^​(Z,X) and q^​=ϕ(Z,X,p^​(Z,X)), while p​^​, p​^​, q^​tr, min{p​^​(X),q^​(Z,X)}, and (q^​(Z,X)−p​^​(X))+​ are obtained by substituting these estimates into the corresponding definitions. We clip estimated propensity scores and nuisance predictions to their known supports.
We state the convergence rate under high-level nuisance-rate assumptions: (4.8) is well defined for any nuisance estimators trained on I0​∪I1​. 3 then provides one concrete construction, and Corollary O5.1 establishes its rate under conditions on those particular learners, collected in O5 of the Online Appendix.
Assumption 4.9 (Targeted Nuisance Rates).
Conditional on the training samples I0​∪I1​, suppose:
  1. Each of the three maps entering the boundary integral and the trivial tail,
    Λ∈{ p​(X),  min{p​(X),q(Z,X)},  (q(Z,X)−p​(X))+​ },
    satisfies
    EZ,X​[​Λ^−Λ​ ​ I0​,I1​]=OP​(re,n​),
    with re,n​→0.
  2. The clipped estimator g^​1​ satisfies the target-evaluation rate
    EZ,X​[∣g^​1​(q^​tr(Z,X),X)−g1​(qtr(Z,X),X)∣+∣g^​1​(P^,X)−g1​(P,X)∣ ​ I0​,I1​]=OP​(rg,n​).​
    Here rg,n​→0.
  3. Let μ^​1,p​∣x​ be the estimated treated boundary law with quantile function Q​1,p​∣x​. It satisfies the target-weighted rate
    EX​[p​(X)W1​(μ^​1,p​∣X​,μ1,p​∣X​) ​ I0​,I1​]=OP​(rμ,n​).
    Here rμ,n​→0.
Part (1) controls the two limits of the boundary integral and the positive-part tail, averaged under the target distribution. Part (2) addresses the more demanding generated-regressor problem. The estimated propensity score plays two roles: P^ is used in place of the latent index P when learning g1​, and it determines the random arguments at which g^​1​ is evaluated. Part (3) controls the boundary OT contribution in its natural loss. Indeed, in one dimension W1​ equals the integrated absolute quantile error, so this assumption essentially requires that the estimated boundary quantile function Q​1,p​∣x​ converge in L1​ to the true boundary quantile function Q1,p​∣x​, weighted by the target p​(X).
Theorem 4.10 (Nonparametric Convergence Rate).
Suppose Assumption 2.1, Assumption 3.6, and Assumption 4.9 hold. Then
∣θ​^​ω,1​−θ​ω,1​∣=OP​(n−1/2+re,n​+rg,n​+rμ,n​).
Theorem 4.10 provides a high-level theoretical guarantee, and B.3 gives a concrete construction: on I0​ we regress W on (Z,X); on I1​ we estimate g1​ by boundary-adaptive local-linear smoothing in the scalar index P combined with a flexible regression in X, and we estimate the treated boundary law by conditional quantile regression on the treated observations whose estimated propensity lies within δn​ of the estimated lower boundary. Under conditions (L1)–(L3), Corollary O5.1 relates its learner errors to the target error:
∣θ​^​ω,1​−θ​ω,1​∣=OP​(n−1/2+rp,n​+rg,loc,n​+rQ,n​+δn​+εn​+MQ−1​),
where rp,n​ is a sup-norm first-stage rate, rg,loc,n​ is an L1​ prediction rate for g^​1​ at the two arguments at which the target evaluates it, and rQ,n​ is a p​(X)-weighted L1​ rate for the conditional quantile fit relative to the law selected by the estimated boundary window. The threshold-crossing model gives the linear localization error δn​+rp,n​ directly; εn​ and MQ−1​ are the trimmed quantile-tail and grid-interpolation errors.
Applying the same construction to the reversed system W0=1−W, P0=1−P, q0=1−q, U0=1−U gives the untreated component, and the two bounds for the full PRTE converge at the maximum of the two componentwise rates; see B.3.

5 Simulation

We validate our theoretical results through synthetic experiments and a real-data empirical application. All experiments compare our method (hereafter IVOT) bounds against the moment-relaxation bounds of Mogstad et~al. (2018) (hereafter IVMTE). Detailed numerical tables, the full data-generating processes, and additional results are deferred to O6 of the Online Appendix.

5.1 Synthetic Experiments

We consider three synthetic settings: one with a continuous instrument, one with a discrete instrument, and one with a discrete instrument and covariates, each using a distinct data-generating process (DGP). Throughout the target is θα​:=E[Yqα​−Y] under the policy qα​=clip(p+α,0,1); the first two designs report α∈[−0.12,0.12], and the covariate design a window of larger shifts. We give IVMTE a flexible, near-nonparametric u-spline sieve. O6 gives the DGPs and the comparison choices; the replication package lists the numerical settings.
Continuous instrument. The continuous-instrument DGP uses a logistic propensity p(Z)=logistic(−1+2Z) with limited support p(Z)∈[0.27,0.73] and a constant marginal treatment effect MTE(u)=0.5; since p(Z)+α never leaves [0,1] on the reported grid, the ground truth is exactly θα​=0.5α. 2 shows the identified sets at n=5,000, together with the population sharp set, which is closed form here because both potential-outcome means are affine in u; O6 of the Online Appendix derives it and confirms the formula numerically using a discretized linear program built from the primitive problem (3.2). IVOT is tighter at every grid point, by a width ratio ranging from 3.4× at ∣α∣=0.12 to 23.3× at ∣α∣=0.01, and the true θα​ falls inside the IVOT interval at 24 of the 25 grid points. The IVMTE bounds are markedly asymmetric—at α=0.05 the upper bound reaches twice the truth while the lower bound crosses zero. The single miss is at α=0.01, where the sharp set is itself only 4×10−4 wide: the unscaled identified-set width is of order α2 near zero, so small estimation errors can displace the interval away from the truth. O6 reports a 20-replication study of the inclusion rate.
Discrete instrument. The discrete-instrument DGP uses Z∼Bernoulli(0.5) with two-point propensity score {0.25,0.75}, to which the closed-form bounds of Theorem 3.4 apply, and a heterogeneous MTE(u)=0.48+0.18u. The outcome support is [0,1.08] and the exact policy-effect truth is θα​=0.57α+0.09α2; both are derived in O6. 3 shows the identified sets at n=5,000 alongside the population sharp set. The truth falls inside the IVOT interval at all 25 grid points, and the IVOT interval is 2.4–3.6× narrower than IVMTE throughout: at α=0.05 the IVOT interval is [−0.001,0.042] (width 0.043) versus the IVMTE interval [−0.051,0.054] (width 0.105). The gap between the two methods is enough to change the qualitative conclusion at large shifts: the estimated IVMTE identified set contains zero at every α, whereas the estimated IVOT identified set excludes zero once α⩾0.08.
Discrete instrument with covariates. The third design adds five continuous covariates to a three-valued instrument, with MTE(u,x) varying in both arguments, and is built so that Assumption 4.2 holds exactly with cgap​=0.04 and every component of the score is active on the reported window α∈[0.195,0.255], at n=4,000. As in the two designs above the comparison is against IVMTE in its nonparametric form, so the u-spline sieve is interacted with the covariates and the MTR is left unrestricted in shape as well as in level. O6 of the Online Appendix gives the DGP, the policy window, the comparison choices, and the numerical tables.
4 shows the estimated IVOT interval tracking the population sharp set—closed form here up to the expectation over X—and containing the truth at all 11 grid points, at 0.79–1.06 times the sharp width. IVOT is narrower than IVMTE by 1.10–1.46× at degree 3 and 1.34–1.78× at degree 7, and the difference is qualitative: at α=0.219 the sharp set is [0.019,0.134] and IVOT [0.015,0.137], while IVMTE at degree 7 returns [−0.012,0.156]. Both that interval and its pointwise 95% backward confidence band contain zero throughout the policy-shift grid, so the moment relaxation loses the sign of the policy effect.
The estimation theory of 4 is tested separately by Monte Carlo. Over 400 replications at each of five sample sizes from 1,000 to 16,000 the sampling standard deviation contracts at the parametric rate, the estimated standard errors closely match the Monte Carlo standard deviations at the larger sample sizes—their ratios rise to 1.00 and 1.02 for the two bounds—and the level-set recovery step returns the correct configuration in every replication once n⩾8,000. O6 of the Online Appendix gives the full Monte Carlo results.

5.2 Effect of Price Subsidies for Bed Nets

Background and setup. We apply our method to the bed net subsidy experiment of Dupas (2014). The policy question is how the price of a bed net affects its usage, which is what a PRTE measures. For n=1,078 Kenyan households the data contain the offered price as instrument Z (17 values spanning 0–250 KSh, randomized across distribution points), purchase as treatment W, and one-year follow-up usage as outcome Y. We compare two fixed-price policies: the baseline assigns every household the reference price z0​=150 KSh, and for each α∈[0.05,0.62] the alternative raises the purchase propensity from p^​(z0​) to qα​:=min(p^​(z0​)+α,1). The target is PRTEα​=E[Yqα​−Yp(z0​)]/α; because both policies are constant in Z, the mean policy shift equals α exactly, so the denominator is the shift size rather than an estimated quantity. The baseline is the fixed-price policy Yp(z0​), not the observed Y under randomized prices, and the grid is itself constructed from the first stage, its endpoint αmax​≈0.621 being the estimated propensity at zero price minus the estimated baseline propensity. Because the instrument is discrete, the closed-form bounds of Theorem 3.4 apply directly to the numerator, after which we divide by α. For IVMTE, we approximate the marginal treatment response (MTR) functions with degree-10 and degree-20 u-spline sieves on [0,1]. Full data, propensity-estimation, and policy-construction details are in O6.
Results. 5 plots the IVOT and IVMTE identified sets for PRTEα​ across subsidy levels. IVOT consistently yields a tighter identified set than IVMTE across the reported range of α and at both spline degrees. At the smallest subsidy (α=0.05), the IVOT interval is 3.3 times narrower than IVMTE at degree 10 and 5.3 times narrower at degree 20.
Both methods indicate a positive policy effect across most of the subsidy range—the IVOT lower bound is positive throughout, and the degree-10 IVMTE lower bound is positive for all α, with the more conservative degree-20 lower bound turning positive once α⩾0.14. IVOT achieves near-point identification (width <0.05) for the majority of α values. Those narrow identified sets do not translate one-for-one into narrower confidence intervals. O6 gives more details and explanations for the wide confidence intervals.

6 Conclusion

We connected the partial identification of PRTEs in IV models to OT: formulating it as a CCOT problem over the joint laws compatible with the observed data, we showed that the multidimensional optimization reduces analytically to one-dimensional OT problems with product costs, yielding closed-form sharp bounds and bypassing the numerical optimization that existing computational approaches require. In a companion note we replace threshold crossing by a conditional quantile representation of the selection equation and obtain sharp closed-form bounds for continuous and multi-valued treatments, under a rank-overlap condition in the strictly monotonic case and an algebraic condition on the instrument-induced latent intervals in the ordered-choice case. The estimation theory developed here is for binary treatments, delivering n​-consistency and asymptotic normality with discrete instruments under the stated regularity conditions, and nonparametric convergence rates with continuous ones.
The central insight, demonstrated theoretically and empirically, is that preserving full distributional information is tractable and valuable for tight partial identification: moment-relaxation approaches reduce the observed data to conditional expectations and can produce substantially wider bounds, whereas CCOT enforces compatibility with the entire observed distribution while keeping the optimization transparent. We expect this to extend beyond the IV setting studied here.

On each fixed instrument component C, continuity and common support identify the propensity extrema with the conditional essential extrema of P given (X,Z∈C), which are measurable in x.
