B Estimation Procedure Details

This appendix collects the estimation procedures in full: the three algorithms described in prose in 4 (1, 2, 3) and their nuisance-estimation steps. The closed-form rewritings (4.1) and (4.7) that these procedures start from are stated as Proposition 4.3, Proposition 4.4, Proposition 4.8 in 4; their derivations are purely algebraic and are given in O3 of the Online Appendix.

B.1 Discrete Instrument, Continuous Outcome: Nuisance Estimation

1 states the estimation procedure, and the remainder of this subsection gives the nuisance-estimation steps in full.
Randomly partition the observed dataset of size n into two disjoint sets: an auxiliary sample I1​ and a main estimation sample I2​, each of size n/2. We first estimate p and q on I1​, use the covariates in I2​ only to recover their finite level sets, and then fit all remaining nuisance functions on I1​ given those sets.
  1. Propensity Scores: Estimate the baseline propensity score p(z,x) by regressing the treatment W on covariates X conditional on each z∈Z. Clip p^​(z,x) to [0,1], then compute q^​(z,x)=ϕ(z,x,p^​(z,x)).
  2. Level Sets: Using all covariates in I2​, compute
    pˉ​2​(z)=∣I2​∣1​i∈I2​∑​p^​(z,Xi​),qˉ​2​(z)=∣I2​∣1​i∈I2​∑​q^​(z,Xi​).
    Choose a deterministic threshold ρn​↓0 such that n1/4ρn​→∞. Define S0​={z:pˉ​2​(z)⩽ρn​} and remove the corresponding baseline vertices from the clustering graph. Form an undirected graph from the remaining baseline vertices and all policy vertices. Connect two vertices when the corresponding scalar values among {pˉ​2​(z),qˉ​2​(z):z∈Z} differ by less than cgap​/2, and define the estimated positive score levels as the graph's connected components. The baseline sets Sk​, k⩾1, collect instruments whose remaining (p,z) vertices share a component, ordered by their component averages. The policy sets Tj,k​ collect instruments whose (q,z) vertices share a component and are indexed by the baseline bin containing that component average, using the half-open bins for k<K and the closed final bin for k=K.
  3. Baseline Levels, Instrument Assignment, and Pooled Policy Levels: Given the recovered sets, return to I1​. Set p^​0​(x)≡0. For k=1,…,K, estimate
    pk​(x)=E[W∣Z∈Sk​,X=x],πk​(x)=Pobs​(Z∈Sk​∣X=x)
    by regressing W and 1(Z∈Sk​), respectively, on X; no p0​ or π0​ regression is fitted. For every nonempty Tj,k​, estimate τj,k​(x)=P(Z∈Tj,k​∣X=x) and estimate the within-set assignment shares aj,k​(z,x)=P(Z=z∣Z∈Tj,k​,X=x) jointly with a simplex-valued multinomial learner. Thus a^j,k​(z,x)⩾0 and ∑z∈Tj,k​​a^j,k​(z,x)=1. Clip π^k​ and τ^j,k​ to [cπ​/2,1]. Form the pooled level by the plug-in identity
    qj,k​(x)=E[q(Z,x)∣Z∈Tj,k​,X=x]
    and its sample analog q^​j,k​(x)=∑z∈Tj,k​​a^j,k​(z,x)q^​(z,x). At the population law, every q(z,x) in Tj,k​ equals qj,k​(x), so pooling preserves the boundary while giving it a regular extension when estimated instrument-specific levels are not exactly tied. Estimate the two conditional probabilities defining γfull,k​ from their respective set indicators, clip each estimate to [0,1], and subtract. Estimate γj,k​ and the tail weight
    γK​(x):=Pobs​(Z∈j=1⋃lK​​Tj,K​​X=x)
    from their set indicators and also clip them to [0,1].
  4. Conditional Quantiles: Set the structural lower-boundary value ν0,k​(x)≡ymin​. For j=1,…,lk​, νj,k​(x)=QY,k∣x​(κj,k​(x)) is the κj,k​(x)-quantile of the conditional distribution μ1,k∣x​, where μ1,k∣x​ is identified in (3.17). Applying the quantile characterization Pμ1,k∣x​​(Y⩽νj,k​(x))=κj,k​(x)=pk+1​(x)−pk​(x)qj,k​(x)−pk​(x)​ and expanding Pμ1,k∣x​​ in terms of the observed conditional distributions yields the following moment equation:
    pk+1​(X)​E[1(Y⩽νj,k​(X))∣X,Z∈Sk+1​,W=1]−pk​(X)E[1(Y⩽νj,k​(X))∣X,Z∈Sk​,W=1]−(qj,k​(X)−pk​(X))=0.​
    For j=1,…,lk​, we estimate νj,k​ by
    νj,k​(x)​=argνmin​E[Ω(Z,X,W)max{0,ν(X)−Y}−(qj,k​(X)−pk​(X))ν(X)],​
    where
    Ω(Z,X,W)=W⋅(πk+1​(X)1(Z∈Sk+1​)​−πk​(X)1(Z∈Sk​)​),
    with the second term omitted when k=0. Clip each fitted ν^j,k​ to [ymin​,ymax​]. At j=0, q0,k​≡pk​ and κ0,k​=0, so the displayed moment equation does not point-identify a quantile: every value below the essential infimum solves it. The fixed convention ν0,k​=ymin​ removes this nonidentified nuisance. Under the no-atom condition at ymin​ used for the continuous-outcome score, M0,k±​=0 and the associated indicator residuals vanish, so the score is invariant to this boundary convention. By part (ii) of Assumption 4.2, every nonempty policy set in a nonfinal bin has qj,k​>pk​ and therefore corresponds to a regular estimated threshold with j⩾1; the structural threshold ν0,k​ is never estimated. Then, we estimate the conditional expectations of the indicators within the moment constraints:
    Mj,k+​(X)Mj,k−​(X)​:=E[1(Y⩽νj,k​(X))∣Z∈Sk+1​,W=1,X],:=E[1(Y⩽νj,k​(X))∣Z∈Sk​,W=1,X].​
    The minus-side regression is estimated only for k⩾1; at k=0 it is omitted under the structural-boundary convention.
  5. Estimate Jj,k​(X) and Jfull,k​(X): We estimate Jj,k​(x) by
    Jj,k+​(X)Jj,k−​(X)Jj,k​(X)​=E[Y1(νj,k​(X)<Y⩽νj+1,k​(X))∣X,Z∈Sk+1​,W=1],=E[Y1(νj,k​(X)<Y⩽νj+1,k​(X))∣X,Z∈Sk​,W=1],=pk+1​(X)Jj,k+​(X)−pk​(X)Jj,k−​(X),​
    and estimate Jfull,k​(X) by
    Jfull,k+​(X)Jfull,k−​(X)Jfull,k​(X)​=E[Y∣X,Z∈Sk+1​,W=1],=E[Y∣X,Z∈Sk​,W=1],=pk+1​(X)Jfull,k+​(X)−pk​(X)Jfull,k−​(X).​
    For k=0, the two minus-side regressions in these displays are omitted and their products with p0​ are set to zero.
In summary, the freely estimated nuisance functions are
η(x)={p(z,x),pk​(x),πk​(x),τj,k​(x),aj,k​(z,x),γfull,k​(x),γj,k​(x),γK​(x),νj,k​(x),Mj,k±​(x),Jj,k±​(x),Jfull,k±​(x)}j,k​.​
Here πk​ and every minus-side object are included only for k⩾1, while νj,k​ is estimated only for j⩾1; the boundary values given above are fixed.
The Neyman-orthogonal score for the target (4.1) is constructed by combining empirical influence functions for the conditional expectations Jj,k±​(X) and Jfull,k±​(X) with pathwise derivatives arising from the quantile thresholds νj,k​(X) and propensity score boundaries pk​(X). In addition, the score must correct for the estimation of (i) the conditional quantile indicators Mj,k±​(X) via their Riesz representers, (ii) the propensity scores pk​(X) through IPW residuals, and (iii) the alternative policy values qj,k​(X) through the derivative ∂p∂ϕ​. The weighting regressions γ(X) are handled by forming product scores using the chain rule for influence functions. The complete formulas for all score components—ψj,kJ​, ψfull,kJ​, ψj,kprod​, ψfull,kprod​, and ψΔK​​—are given in C.1.

B.2 Discrete Instrument, Binary Outcome: Nuisance Estimation

The closed-form reduction (4.4) is proved as part (ii) of Proposition 4.4 in O3.2 of the Online Appendix. 2 states the estimation procedure, and the remainder of this subsection gives the full nuisance-estimation steps.
The procedure follows the same two-step sample-splitting strategy as the continuous outcome case, but with a simpler nuisance list: the conditional quantile estimation (Step 4 of the continuous-outcome procedure) and the indicator expectations Mj,k±​ are no longer needed. The full nuisance list, for all interval indices k∈{0,…,K} and sub-interval indices j∈{0,…,lk​}, is
η(x)={p(z,x),pk​(x),πk​(x),τj,k​(x),aj,k​(z,x),γfull,k​(x),γj,k​(x),γK​(x),P1,k​(x)}j,k​.
Step 1: Nuisance Estimation.
  1. Propensity Scores, Level Sets, and Assignment Probabilities: Follow Steps 1–3 of B.1: estimate p^​(z,x) and q^​(z,x) on I1​; construct Sk​,Tj,k​ from pˉ​2​,qˉ​2​ using the covariates in I2​; then, given those sets, fit p^​k​, π^k​, τ^j,k​, a^j,k​, the pooled q^​j,k​, the two conditional probabilities entering γ^​full,k​, and the probability nuisances γ^​j,k​,γ^​K​ on I1​. Form γ^​full,k​ by subtracting its two constituent probability estimates. Set p^​0​≡0, fit no π0​, and clip all conditional probability estimates to [0,1], with π^k​,τ^j,k​ clipped further to [cπ​/2,1].
  2. Conditional Joint Probability: Set P^1,0​(x)=0. For k=1,…,K, estimate P1,k​(x)=E[YW∣Z∈Sk​,X=x] on I1​ by regressing YW on X conditional on Z∈Sk​, using any flexible machine learning method, and clip the fitted conditional probabilities to [0,1].
  3. Rearrangement: Set the structural boundary value P^1,0​(x)=P^1,0∗​(x)=0. In the population, P1,k​(X) is monotone non-decreasing in k because Jfull,k​(X)=P1,k+1​(X)−P1,k​(X)⩾0. Because the P^1,k​ are fitted on different instrument subsets, finite-sample estimates need not preserve monotonicity. Clip them to [0,1], sort only (P^1,1​(Xi​),…,P^1,K​(Xi​)) to obtain (P^1,1∗​(Xi​),…,P^1,K∗​(Xi​)), and retain the fixed zero boundary. Define J^full,k​=P^1,k+1∗​−P^1,k∗​ and use this same rearranged P^∗ vector in every score plug-in and residual; no separate gap projection is applied.
The identification formulas allow a nonempty policy set to lie at qj,k​=pk​. For the displayed inference formulas, part (ii) of Assumption 4.2 excludes this collision in nonfinal bins, so the regular residual Rq,j,k​ never represents the same boundary as the structural convention q0,k​=pk​.
Step 2: Neyman-Orthogonal Score Construction. The target functional for the lower bound is θ​ω,1​=E[m(X;η)], where
m(X;η)=k=0∑K−1​(γfull,k​(X)Jfull,k​(X)+j=1∑lk​​γj,k​(X)hj,k−​(X))+ΔK​(X),
and the Neyman-orthogonal score takes the aggregated form
ψ(O;η)​=k=0∑K−1​(ψfull,kprod​(O;η)+j=1∑lk​​ψj,kprod​(O;η))+ψΔK​​(O;η).​(B.1)​
The construction of each component score proceeds by computing the pathwise derivatives of hj,k−​(X) with respect to P1,k​(X), pk​(X), and qj,k​(X), and combining them with standard IPW residuals. Because hj,k−​ involves a max operator, the pathwise derivatives depend on active-set, boundary, and dominance indicators that track which constraint binds in the max. The product scores account for the estimation of γ(X) via the chain rule for influence functions, and the trivial-bound score ψΔK​​ is identical to the continuous-outcome case. The complete formulas are given in C.2. Averaging the plug-in scores over I2​ yields the estimator previewed in (4.5); the upper-bound score is derived similarly.

B.3 Continuous Instrument: Localized g1​ and Boundary Quantile Estimation

We give the details behind 3. Randomly partition the data into a propensity sample I0​, a nuisance sample I1​, and an evaluation sample I2​, with ∣Ij​∣/n→ρj​∈(0,1) for j=0,1,2. Estimating p on I0​ makes every localization rule used on I1​ fixed conditional on I0​. The selected observations are therefore conditionally i.i.d. Cross-fitting repeats the construction over several partitions and averages the resulting scores.
Propensity scores, support, and policy. On I0​, regress W on (Z,X) and clip the fitted values to [0,1]. Set q^​(z,x)=ϕ(z,x,p^​(z,x)) and compute
p​^​(x)=z∈Zinf​p^​(z,x),p​^​(x)=z∈Zsup​p^​(z,x),q^​tr(z,x)=min{p​^​(x),max{p​^​(x),q^​(z,x)}}.
Conditional expectation g1​ via localized local-linear learning. The target evaluates g1​(u,x)=E[YW∣P=u,X=x] at the boundaries of the conditional support. A local-constant regression generally has first-order boundary bias. We instead use a local-linear fit in the scalar index and allow flexible learners in x, following the same localization principle as local-polynomial DR-learning [Kennedy, 2023] and generalized random forests [Athey et~al., 2019].
Let Khn​​(t)=K(t/hn​)/hn​, set P^i​=p^​(Zi​,Xi​), and take a grid um​=m/Mg​, m=0,…,Mg​. At each grid point, Step 3 of 3 fits functions (g^​1​(um​,⋅),β^​m​) on I1​ by
(g^​1​(um​,⋅),β^​m​)∈argg,β∈Fn​min​i∈I1​∑​Khn​​(P^i​−um​)[Yi​Wi​−g(Xi​)−β(Xi​)(P^i​−um​)]2.
Here Fn​ is a user-chosen class of functions of x. With a linear class, the display is weighted least squares on the augmented design (1,x,P^i​−um​,(P^i​−um​)x). The fitted intercept g^​1​(um​,x) estimates g1​(um​,x). Define g^​1​(u,x) between grid points by linear interpolation, and then clip it to the known range of YW. For u∈[um​,um+1​],
g^​1​(u,x)=g^​1​(um​,x)+um+1​−um​u−um​​(g^​1​(um+1​,x)−g^​1​(um​,x)).
Condition (L2) of Assumption O5.2 controls its prediction error only at the two estimated arguments used by the target.
Treated boundary law. Equation (4.6) shows that the required distribution is the normalized canonical treated submeasure at P=p​(X), equivalently the one-sided boundary limit of the treated outcome law. Choose δn​→0 and form
Iδ,1​={i∈I1​:Wi​=1, P^i​≤p​^​(Xi​)+δn​}.
Conditional on I0​, this is an i.i.d. selected sample. On the quantile grid τm​=m/MQ​, m=1,…,MQ​−1, estimate the conditional quantiles of Y given X on this sample by check-function regression over a function class FQ​,
Q​(τm​∣⋅)∈argf∈FQ​min​i∈Iδ,1​∑​ρτm​​(Yi​−f(Xi​)),ρτ​(u)=u(τ−1(u<0)).(B.2)

F Worked Examples

This section works through two examples that illustrate the identification results of 3: a binary-instrument calculation that makes the three-part decomposition behind Theorem 3.4 explicit, and a comparison quantifying how much wider the moment-relaxation bounds can be.

F.1 Illustrative Example for Theorem 3.4

Example O2.1.
Consider a binary instrument with P(Z=1)=1/2 and a constant propensity score p(0)=p(1)=1/2. Let the target weight function be ω(u)=E[1(u∈(0,q1​(Z)))], where q1​(0)=1/4 and q1​(1)=3/4.
Simple calculation gives the explicit piecewise form of the weight function:
ω(u)=⎩⎨⎧​1,1/2,0,​if u∈(0,1/4]if u∈(1/4,3/4]if u∈(3/4,1]​​

Plugging this into our closed-form optimal transport solution, the sharp lower bound elegantly decomposes into three distinct economic components. On I0​, the optimal coupling pairs the highest weights in ω(u) with the lowest quantiles of the observed outcome distribution Y∣W=1. For the unconstrained interval I1​, because ω(u)⩾0 here, the optimal solution trivially assigns the logical minimum ymin​.
Evaluating the integral exactly yields:
θ​ω,1​​=∫01/2​QY∣W=1​(2u)ω(u)du+∫1/21​ymin​ω(u)du=Identifiable Mean41​E[Y∣W=1]​​ + Optimal Transport (CVaR)81​CVaR0.5​(Y∣W=1)​​ + Trivial Lower Bound81​ymin​​​​(48)​
where CVaRα​(Y)=α1​∫0α​QY​(s)ds is the lower-tail Conditional Value at Risk. The integral allocates exactly probability α to the tail, including the appropriate fraction of any atom at its cutoff.
This decomposition also makes precise what is lost under moment relaxation. Moment relaxation enforces only the first moment over the entire observed interval: E[m1​(U)∣U∈(0,1/2)]=E[Y∣W=1].
To minimize the objective, their linear program evaluates:
m1​min​(41​E[Y∣W=1]+21​∫01/4​m1​(u)du)+81​ymin​​
subject to the moment constraint and the box restriction ymin​⩽m1​(u)⩽ymax​. Writing E1​=E[Y∣W=1], these restrictions imply

F.2 Comparison with Moment Relaxation Approach

Example O2.2 (Comparison with Moment Relaxation Approach).
Suppose there are no covariates and the weight function is ω(u)=1(u∈(1/4,1/2)). Our target parameter simplifies to:
E[(Y(1)−Y(0))1(U∈(1/4,1/2))].
Consider a data-generating process with a binary instrument Z∈{0,1}, propensity scores p(0)=1/4 and p(1)=3/4, and the observed outcome is constantly zero, Y(w)=0 almost surely for w∈{0,1}.
Under our CCOT formulation, this parameter is point-identified and its value is exactly 0. Because the conditional distribution of the observed outcome is a Dirac measure at zero, P(Y∈⋅∣W=1,Z=z)=δ0​(⋅) for each z, the observational constraint forces π1​(⋅∣u)=δ0​ for almost all u∈(0,3/4). Similarly, P(Y∈⋅∣W=0,Z=z)=δ0​(⋅) forces π0​(⋅∣u)=δ0​ for almost all u∈(1/4,1). Since ω is supported on (1/4,1/2)⊂(0,3/4)∩(1/4,1), both Y(1) and Y(0) are point-identified on the support of ω, and the target is sharply 0.
In contrast, Mogstad et~al. (2018) relax the distributional constraints into moment constraints on the MTR, defined as mw​(u)=E[Y(w)∣U=u]. Under their framework, the data restrict the MTR only through its conditional expectation:
p(z)1​∫0p(z)​m1​(u)du1−p(z)1​∫p(z)1​m0​(u)du​=E[Y∣W=1,Z=z]=0,=E[Y∣W=0,Z=z]=0.​
Evaluating at z=0 and z=1 gives the four constraints
∫01/4​m1​=∫03/4​m1​=0,∫1/41​m0​=∫3/41​m0​=0,
or equivalently, after differencing,
∫01/4​m1​=0,∫1/43/4​m1​=0,∫3/41​m0​=0,∫1/43/4​m0​=0.
Their method bounds the target parameter by solving:
m0​,m1​∈Mmax​/m0​,m1​∈Mmin​s.t.​∫1/41/2​(m1​(u)−m0​(u))du∫01/4​m1​=∫1/43/4​m1​=0,∫3/41​m0​=∫1/43/4​m0​=0.​
If the function class M is sufficiently rich, this relaxation discards the point-mass nature of the outcome and yields unnecessarily wide bounds. The moment constraints only pin the integral of each MTR over (1/4,3/4) to zero, but leave the shape within this interval unrestricted. An adversarial optimizer exploits this by setting m1​(u)=M on (1/4,1/2) and m1​(u)=−M on (1/2,3/4), leaving m1​≡0 on (0,1/4); this satisfies every constraint above yet contributes M/4 to the objective. Applying the symmetric construction to m0​ yields a total upper bound of M/2 instead of 0. Across the family of known outcome bounds [−M,M], the resulting moment bounds [−M/2,M/2] grow with M, while the distributional sharp value remains 0. By strictly enforcing the full distributional constraint, the CCOT approach eliminates these mathematically feasible but structurally impossible counterfactuals. 7 illustrates this gap numerically.

EX​​[p​(X)∫01​Q1,p​∣X​(u)ω(X,p​(X)u)du]=EZ,X​[p​(X)∫01​Q1,p​∣X​(u)(1(p​(X)u⩽q(Z,X))−1)du]=−EZ,X​[∫min{p​(X),q(Z,X)}p​(X)​Q1,p​∣X​(v/p​(X))dv].​
Both sides are zero when p​(X)=0, which justifies the convention in the proposition.
Second term (g1​ difference on the LIV interval). The structural integral representation gives g1​(u,x)=∫0u​E[Y(1)∣U=s,X=x]ds, so g1​(⋅,x) is absolutely continuous. Hence, for any r∈[0,1],
∫p​(X)p​(X)​∂u​g1​(u,X)1(u≤r)du=g1​(min{p​(X),max{p​(X),r}},X)−g1​(p​(X),X).
Applying this identity first with r=q(Z,X) and then with r=P is essential when q(Z,X)<p​(X). Since P∈[p​(X),p​(X)], the two lower-endpoint terms cancel and give
EX​[∫p​(X)p​(X)​∂u∂g1​(u,X)​ω(X,u)du]​=EZ,X​[g1​(qtr(Z,X),X)−g1​(P,X)].​
Third term (trivial bound on (p​(X),1]). Since P≤p​(X), the baseline indicator vanishes on this tail and ω(X,u)=P(u≤q(Z,X)∣X)≥0. Therefore
ymin​EX​[∫p​(X)1​ω(X,u)du]=ymin​EZ,X​[(q(Z,X)−p​(X))+​].​
Aggregating the three components yields (4.7). The upper-bound representation replaces the countermonotonic boundary coupling by the comonotonic coupling and swaps ymin​ for ymax​ in the trivial tail.
∎

H Moment Condition and Neyman Orthogonality of the Discrete-Instrument Scores

This section proves Lemma D.1. Both parts are term-by-term calculations that repeatedly apply the tower property to inverse-probability-weighted residuals with zero conditional mean.
Throughout, η0​ denotes the vector of true nuisance parameter values and θ0​=θ​ω,1​ the true parameter value. For a functional Φ(η) and a perturbation direction δ in the same function space as η, we write ∂δ​Φ(η):=dtd​Φ(η+tδ)​t=0​ for the Gateaux (directional) derivative; when the perturbation is along a single nuisance component ηα​, we write ∂ηα​​ for brevity.

H.1 Continuous Outcome

Recall the target functional:
θ0​=E[k=0∑K−1​(γfull,k​(X)Jfull,k​(X)+j=1∑lk​​γj,k​(X)Jj−1,k​(X))+ΔK​(X)],(O4.1)
and the total Neyman-orthogonal score assembled from the components of C.1:
ψ(O;η)=k=0∑K−1​(ψfull,kprod​(O;η)+j=1∑lk​​ψj,kprod​(O;η))+ψΔK​​(O;η),(O4.2)
where each product score debiases the corresponding term in the target. Specifically, ψj,kJ​(O;η) is the uncentered orthogonal score for the conditional integral component E[Jj,k​(X)], and the product score for E[γj,k​(X)Jj−1,k​(X)] is:
ψj,kprod​(O;η)=γj,k​(X)ψj−1,kJ​(O;η)+Jj−1,k​(X)(1(Z∈⋃l=jlk​​Tl,k​)−γj,k​(X)),(O4.3)
and symmetrically for ψfull,kprod​(O;η).
Proof of Lemma D.1(i).
Moment condition. We show E[ψ(O;η0​)]=θ0​. All influence function correction terms in the score are inverse-probability-weighted residuals of the general form
πk​(X)1(Z∈Sk​)​W(g(Y,X)−E[g(Y,X)∣X,Z∈Sk​,W=1]).
By the tower property, conditioning first on (X,Z): when Z∈Sk​, we have p(Z,X)=pk​(X), so E[W∣X,Z∈Sk​]=pk​(X). It follows that
E[πk​(X)1(Z∈Sk​)​W(g−E[g∣X,Sk​,W=1])]=E[πk​(X)1(Z∈Sk​)​pk​(X)⋅0]=0.
Applying this identity to each correction term, E[IFJ±​(O)]=0 and E[IFMj,k±​​(O)]=0 at η0​. The quantile correction term in ψj,kJ​ contains the factor pk+1​(X)Mj,k+​(X)−pk​(X)Mj,k−​(X)−(qj,k​(X)−pk​(X)), which vanishes at η0​ by the conditional moment equation
​pk+1​(X)E[1(Y⩽νj,k​(X))∣X,Sk+1​,W=1]−pk​(X)E[1(Y⩽νj,k​(X))∣X,Sk​,W=1]−(qj,k​(X)−pk​(X))=0​(O4.4)
which defines νj,k​ for j⩾1; the boundary value ν0,k​=ymin​ is fixed. The propensity score correction terms πk​(X)1(Z∈Sk​)​(W−pk​(X)) and the pooled policy-level residuals Rq,j,k​ likewise have zero mean by the same tower-property argument. Consequently,
E[ψj,kJ​(O;η0​)]​=E[Jj,k​(X)],​E[ψfull,kJ​(O;η0​)]​=E[Jfull,k​(X)].​
For the product scores, substituting (O4.3) and using E[1(Z∈⋃l=jlk​​Tl,k​)−γj,k​(X)]=0:
E[ψj,kprod​(O;η0​)]​=E[γj,k​(X)=Jj−1,k​(X)E[ψj−1,kJ​(O;η0​)∣X]​​]+E[Jj−1,k​(X)=0E[1(⋯)−γj,k​(X)∣X]​​]=E[γj,k​(X)Jj−1,k​(X)],​
and symmetrically E[ψfull,kprod​(O;η0​)]=E[γfull,k​(X)Jfull,k​(X)]. The same reasoning yields E[ψΔK​​(O;η0​)]=E[ΔK​(X)]. Summing over all components and comparing with (O4.1) gives E[ψ(O;η0​)]=θ0​.
Neyman orthogonality of ψj,kJ​. We show that the Gateaux derivative ∂t​E[ψj,kJ​(O;η0​+tδ)]∣t=0​ vanishes for all perturbation directions δ. We group the nuisance parameters by type and check orthogonality with respect to each group.
Conditional expectations (Jj,k±​,Mj,k±​). Consider a perturbation Jj,k+​(X)→Jj,k+​(X)+tδJ+(X). The plug-in term Jj,k​=pk+1​Jj,k+​−pk​Jj,k−​ contributes +E[pk+1​(X)δJ+(X)], while the IPW correction IFJ+​ contributes −E[πk+1​(X)1(Z∈Sk+1​)​pk+1​(X)δJ+(X)]. These cancel because
E[πk+1​(X)1(Z∈Sk+1​)​​X]=πk+1​(X)P(Z∈Sk+1​∣X)​=1.
For Jj,k−​ the plug-in derivative is −pk​δJ−, while differentiating −IFJ−​ gives +pk​δJ−. For Mj,k+​, the plug-in part of the quantile moment gives νj,k​pk+1​δM+ and differentiating νj,k​IFMj,k+​​ gives its negative; the minus-side and j+1 terms cancel in the same way, with their displayed signs. Thus every conditional-expectation direction cancels explicitly.
Instrument assignment probabilities (πk​,πk+1​). Perturbing πk+1​(X)→πk+1​(X)+tδπ(X) introduces a factor −δπ(X)/πk+1​(X)2 in the IPW terms. For any such IPW term 1(Z∈Sk+1​)πk+1​(X)−1W(g(O)−gˉ​(X)), the first-order contribution is
−E[πk+1​(X)21(Z∈Sk+1​)​δπ(X)W(g(O)−gˉ​(X))].
Conditioning on (X,Z) with Z∈Sk+1​, we have E[W(g(O)−gˉ​(X))∣X,Z∈Sk+1​]=pk+1​(X)⋅0=0 at η0​, so the Gateaux derivative vanishes. The argument for δπk​ is identical when k⩾1; there is no π0​ direction.
Propensity scores (pk​,pk+1​). For k⩾1, a perturbation pk​(X)→pk​(X)+tδpk​(X) generates first-order contributions from three sources (all multiplied by δpk​(X) inside E[⋅]). There is no such direction at k=0 because p0​≡0 is fixed:
  1. (i) The plug-in term Jj,k​=pk+1​Jj,k+​−pk​Jj,k−​, contributing −Jj,k−​(X);
  2. (ii) The quantile correction terms νj,k​(⋯)−νj+1,k​(⋯), contributing νj,k​(X)(1(j⩾1)−Mj,k−​(X))−νj+1,k​(X)(1−Mj+1,k−​(X)). At j=0, the first constant is absent because q0,k​−pk​≡0;
  3. (iii) The Riesz representer correction αpk​​(X)πk​(X)1(Z∈Sk​)​(W−pk​(X)), contributing −αpk​​(X).
Substituting the definition
αpk​​=−Jj,k−​−νj,k​Mj,k−​+νj+1,k​Mj+1,k−​+1(j⩾1)νj,k​−νj+1,k​
and collecting terms:
​(−Jj,k−​)+(1(j⩾1)νj,k​−νj,k​Mj,k−​−νj+1,k​+νj+1,k​Mj+1,k−​)−(−Jj,k−​−νj,k​Mj,k−​+νj+1,k​Mj+1,k−​+1(j⩾1)νj,k​−νj+1,k​)=0.​
The calculation for δpk+1​, using αpk+1​​=Jj,k+​+νj,k​Mj,k+​−νj+1,k​Mj+1,k+​, is identical.
Quantile thresholds (νj,k​,νj+1,k​). A perturbation is considered only for estimated thresholds. In particular, ν0,k​=ymin​ is fixed and has no nuisance direction. A perturbation νj,k​(X)→νj,k​(X)+tδν(X) affects the score through two channels.
Channel (a): indicator boundaries. The indicator 1(νj,k​(X)⩽Y) appears inside IFJ±​ and IFMj,k±​​. For a generic relevant conditional law F and at​=ν+tδν, the combined boundary change from the truncated first-moment correction and its quantile-moment correction is, up to its orientation,
∫νat​​(at​−y)dF(y).
If the density of F is bounded by C in the stated neighborhood, then
​∫νat​​(at​−y)dF(y)​⩽C∣at​−ν∣2.
The oriented-integral convention covers at​<ν. Applying this bound to the plus and minus conditional laws shows that the combined boundary contribution is O(t2δν2) and therefore has derivative zero at t=0.
Channel (b): explicit multiplicative factor. The term νj,k​(X)(pk+1​Mj,k+​−pk​Mj,k−​−(qj,k​−pk​)) contributes δν(X) times the conditional moment equation (O4.4), which vanishes at η0​. The dependence of αpk​​ and αpk+1​​ on νj,k​ is absorbed by the zero-mean residuals: for any L2​ function h(X),
E[h(X)πk​(X)1(Z∈Sk​)​(W−pk​(X))]=E[h(X)πk​(X)πk​(X)​⋅0]=0.
The local density bound gives the quadratic control above. The treatment of δνj+1,k​ is symmetric.
Alternative policy propensity (qj,k​). For j⩾1, use the pooled representation qj,k​(X)=E[q(Z,X)∣Z∈Tj,k​,X]. At the population law, all the instrument-specific policy propensities in Tj,k​ equal this common value. Consequently, perturbations of the conditional instrument probabilities have no first-order effect on the pooled value, while perturbing the propensity functions induces
δqj,k​(X)=τj,k​(X)1​z∈Tj,k​∑​π(z,X)∂p∂ϕ​(z,X,p(z,X))δp(z,X).
At j=0, T0,k​=∅ and the boundary q0,k​=pk​ is handled by the corrected pk​ representer above. For j⩾1, the first-order contributions are:
from quantile correctionfrom differentiating the policy residual​:−E[νj,k​(X)δqj,k​(X)],:+E[νj,k​(X)δqj,k​(X)].​
The pooled correction itself has mean zero at the truth. Differentiating its residuals gives
∂t​E[−νj,k​(X)Rq,j,k​(O)]​t=0​=E[νj,k​(X)δqj,k​(X)],
because E[1(Z=z)∣X]=π(z,X). Derivatives of the coefficients multiply zero-mean residuals and therefore vanish. The two displayed contributions cancel, and the treatment of qj+1,k​ is symmetric.
The simplex restriction is essential for the preceding pooled representation. Along a within-set share perturbation aj,k​(z,X)↦aj,k​(z,X)+tδaz​(X), admissible directions satisfy ∑z∈Tj,k​​δaz​(X)=0. Since q(z,X)=qj,k​(X) for every z∈Tj,k​ at the population law,
∂t​z∈Tj,k​∑​(aj,k​(z,X)+tδaz​(X))q(z,X)​t=0​=qj,k​(X)z∈Tj,k​∑​δaz​(X)=0.
With estimated instrument-specific policy values, the remaining share term is ∑z​(a^z​−az​)(q^​(z,X)−qj,k​(X)), a product of two nuisance errors. A perturbation of τj,k​ affects only the factor 1/τj,k​ in Rq,j,k​; its derivative multiplies the conditionally mean-zero numerator ∑z∈Tj,k​​ϕp​(z,X,p(z,X))1(Z=z)(W−p(z,X)) and is therefore zero at the truth.
This establishes orthogonality for ψj,kJ​.
Neyman orthogonality of the remaining components. For ψfull,kJ​, a perturbation of Jfull,k+​ contributes pk+1​δJ+ through the plug-in and −pk+1​δJ+ through its outcome residual. A perturbation of pk+1​ contributes Jfull,k+​δpk+1​ through the plug-in and its negative through the propensity residual. The minus-side terms cancel identically when k⩾1, and denominator perturbations in πk​,πk+1​ multiply conditionally mean-zero residuals. Hence ψfull,kJ​ is orthogonal in every nuisance direction.
For the product scores, we invoke the chain rule for influence functions. The preceding cancellations hold conditionally on X: at η0​, E[ψj−1,kJ​(O;η0​)∣X]=Jj−1,k​(X), and the Gateaux derivative of this conditional moment is zero in every nuisance direction already considered. Moreover, 1(Z∈⋃l=jlk​​Tl,k​)−γj,k​(X) is the conditional influence function for γj,k​(X)=P(Z∈⋃l=jlk​​Tl,k​∣X). Therefore, the product score (O4.3)
ψj,kprod​=γj,k​(X)ψj−1,kJ​(O;η)+Jj−1,k​(X)(1(Z∈⋃l=jlk​​Tl,k​)−γj,k​(X))
is orthogonal for the product functional E[γj,k​(X)Jj−1,k​(X)]. We treat the two groups of nuisance directions separately. First, let ηα​ be any component other than γj,k​. Then γj,k​ and the indicator residual do not vary, so
∂ηα​​E[ψj,kprod​]=E[γj,k​(X)=0∂ηα​​E[ψj−1,kJ​∣X]​​]+E[∂ηα​​Jj−1,k​(X)=0E[1(⋯)−γj,k​(X)∣X]​​]=0,​
where the first expectation vanishes by the conditional orthogonality just established. Second, for the direction γj,k​↦γj,k​+tδγ, the derivative contributions of the explicit prefactor and the residual cancel:
∂t​E[(γj,k​+tδγ)ψj−1,kJ​+Jj−1,k​(1(⋯)−γj,k​−tδγ)]​t=0​=E[δγJj−1,k​]−E[δγJj−1,k​]=0,
using E[ψj−1,kJ​∣X]=Jj−1,k​(X) at η0​. For the full-interval product, the residual is
1(Z∈m=k+1⋃K​l=0⋃lm​​Tl,m​)−1(Z∈m=k+1⋃K​Sm​)−γfull,k​(X),
whose conditional mean is zero by the definition of γfull,k​. Therefore its coefficient and residual derivatives cancel exactly as in (O4.3), even though γfull,k​ is signed.
For ψΔK​​, write
AK​={Z∈⋃j=1lK​​Tj,K​}.
A perturbation of pK​ contributes −ymin​E[γK​(X)δpK​(X)] through the plug-in term and the opposite quantity through differentiation of the pK​ residual. For an instrument-specific direction p(z,X)↦p(z,X)+tδp(z,X), the plug-in derivative is
ymin​E[1(AK​)ϕp​(Z,X,p(Z,X))δp(Z,X)],
and differentiation of the policy residual gives its negative. Perturbations of πK​ and of the coefficient γK​ multiply the conditionally mean-zero pK​ residual, while derivatives of ϕp​ multiply W−p(Z,X) and also have conditional mean zero. Thus every first-order direction in ψΔK​​ cancels.
∎

H.2 Binary Outcome

Proof of Lemma D.1(ii).
Recall the target functional (4.4) and the orthogonal score (B.1), which decomposes as ψ=∑k​(ψfull,kprod​+∑j​ψj,kprod​)+ψΔK​​. Moment condition. We show E[ψ(O;η0​)]=θ0​. The residuals RP,k​ and Rp,k​ have conditional mean zero because P1,k​(X)=E[YW∣Z∈Sk​,X] and pk​(X)=E[W∣Z∈Sk​,X]. The pooled policy residual also satisfies
E[Rq,j,k​(O)∣X]=τj,k​(X)1​z∈Tj,k​∑​ϕp​(z,X,p(z,X))P(Z=z∣X)E[W−p(z,X)∣Z=z,X]=0.​
Thus every correction in ψj,kh​ and ψfull,kJ​ has conditional mean zero, so E[ψj,kh​(O;η0​)∣X]=hj,k−​(X) and E[ψfull,kJ​(O;η0​)∣X]=Jfull,k​(X). Writing Aj,k​={Z∈⋃l=jlk​​Tl,k​}, another application of the tower property gives
E[ψj,kprod​(O;η0​)]​=E[γj,k​(X)E[ψj,kh​(O;η0​)∣X]+hj,k−​(X)E[1(Aj,k​)−γj,k​(X)∣X]]=E[γj,k​(X)hj,k−​(X)].​
The same conditional calculation applies to the full-interval product score. Summing all components therefore gives E[ψ(O;η0​)]=E[m(X;η0​)]=θ0​.
Neyman orthogonality. We must show ∂ηα​​E[ψ(O;η)]​η=η0​​=0 for each nuisance component ηα​. By the product score structure, it suffices to establish orthogonality of the component scores ψj,kh​ and ψfull,kJ​ with respect to (P1,m​,pm​,p(z,X),πm​,τj,k​,aj,k​), and then show that the product scores inherit orthogonality with respect to the γ terms.
Orthogonality of ψj,kh​ with respect to P1,m​. Consider a perturbation P1,m​→P1,m​+tδP1,m​(X). Since hj,k−​ depends on P1,m​ only through Jfull,k​=P1,k+1​−P1,k​, the pathwise derivative is
∂t​E[hj,k−​]​t=0​=E[αP,m(j,k)​(X)δP1,m​(X)],
where αP,k+1(j,k)​=Dj,k−​, αP,k(j,k)​=−Dj,k−​, and αP,m(j,k)​=0 for m∈/{k,k+1}. Under Assumption 4.6, Dj,k−​=1(qj−1,k​<pk+1​−Jfull,k​<qj,k​) is well-defined. The IPW correction Dj,k−​(RP,k+1​−RP,k​) in ψj,kh​ contributes
∂t​E[Dj,k−​(πk+1​1(Z∈Sk+1​)​(YW−P1,k+1​)−πk​1(Z∈Sk​)​(YW−P1,k​))]​t=0​=−E[αP,m(j,k)​δP1,m​],​
using E[πm​1(Z∈Sm​)​∣X]=1, so the two contributions cancel. The same argument gives ∂P1,m​​E[ψfull,kJ​]=0 (with αP,k+1(full,k)​=1 and αP,k(full,k)​=−1).
Orthogonality of ψj,kh​ with respect to pm​ and p(z,X). The propensity scores enter hj,k−​ through three channels:
  1. the integration boundary pk+1​−Jfull,k​, corrected by αp,k+1(j,k)​Rp,k+1​;
  2. the lower level-set boundary q0,k​=pk​ when j=1, corrected by αp,k(1,k)​Rp,k​;
  3. the alternative policy values qj,k​ and qj−1,k​ through the mapping ϕ(z,X,p(z,X)), corrected by the policy terms involving Tj,k​ and Tj−1,k​.
For channel (a), a perturbation pk+1​→pk+1​+tδpk+1​(X) shifts the boundary by δpk+1​, giving ∂t​hj,k−​=−Dj,k−​δpk+1​. The correction αp,k+1(j,k)​Rp,k+1​=−Dj,k−​⋅πk+1​1(Z∈Sk+1​)​(W−pk+1​) contributes ∂t​E[αp,k+1(j,k)​Rp,k+1​]=Dj,k−​δpk+1​, canceling the plug-in derivative.
For channel (b), when j=1 and E1,k−​=1 (i.e., pk​>pk+1​−Jfull,k​), a perturbation of pk​ shifts q0,k​=pk​, giving ∂t​h1,k−​=−E1,k−​I1,k−​δpk​. The correction αp,k(1,k)​Rp,k​ contributes the matching cancellation.
For channel (c), the pooled derivative displayed in the continuous-outcome proof gives ∂t​hj,k−​=Ij,k−​δqj,k​ for the upper boundary. The derivative of Ij,k−​Rq,j,k​ is −Ij,k−​δqj,k​ and therefore cancels it. Symmetrically, when Ej,k−​=1, the correction through Rq,j−1,k​ cancels the derivative through the lower boundary qj−1,k​.
Denominators and within-set shares. A perturbation of πm​ differentiates only denominators in RP,m​ and Rp,m​; each resulting term is a function of X times a conditionally mean-zero residual, so its expectation is zero. The same argument applies to a perturbation of τj,k​ in Rq,j,k​. Finally, admissible share directions satisfy ∑z∈Tj,k​​δaz​(X)=0. At the truth, all q(z,X) in Tj,k​ equal qj,k​(X), and hence
∂t​z∈Tj,k​∑​(aj,k​(z,X)+tδaz​(X))q(z,X)​t=0​=qj,k​(X)z∈Tj,k​∑​δaz​(X)=0.
Thus the simplex-share direction has no first-order effect; with estimated q(z,X) it contributes only the product ∑z​(a^z​−az​)(q^​z​−qj,k​).
Inheritance by product scores. Recall that
ψj,kprod​=γj,k​ψj,kh​+hj,k−​(1(⋯)−γj,k​),E[1(⋯)−γj,k​∣X]=0  at η0​,
while the preceding component-score cancellations hold conditionally on X. Hence any perturbation of a component-score nuisance (P1,m​,pm​,p(z,X),πm​,τj,k​,aj,k​) yields
∂η​E[ψj,kprod​]=E​γj,k​(X)=0∂η​E[ψj,kh​∣X]​​+∂η​hj,k−​(X)=0E[1(⋯)−γj,k​(X)∣X]​​​=0.
For ψfull,kprod​, the same calculation uses the signed residual
1(Z∈m=k+1⋃K​l=0⋃lm​​Tl,m​)−1(Z∈m=k+1⋃K​Sm​)−γfull,k​(X),
whose conditional mean is zero. For ψΔK​​, the pK​ plug-in derivative cancels the derivative of its Rp,K​ correction, while each instrument-specific derivative through q(z,X)=ϕ(z,X,p(z,X)) cancels the corresponding policy residual. Perturbations of πK​, γK​, and the policy-derivative coefficient multiply conditionally mean-zero residuals. Hence ψΔK​​ is also orthogonal in every nuisance direction.
Perturbation of γj,k​ and γfull,k​. The derivative contributions of the two product-score terms cancel. Along γj,k​↦γj,k​+tδγ,
∂t​E[(γj,k​+tδγ)ψj,kh​+hj,k−​(1(⋯)−γj,k​−tδγ)]​t=0​=E[δγE[ψj,kh​∣X]]−E[δγhj,k−​]=0,
because E[ψj,kh​∣X]=hj,k−​(X) at η0​. Replacing the set-indicator residual by the signed residual displayed above gives the identical cancellation for γfull,k​.
∎

I Rate and Learner Conditions for the Concrete Continuous-Instrument Estimator

Theorem 4.10 accepts any nuisance construction satisfying its three target losses. We now express those losses in terms of the learner prediction errors for 3, stated in B.3.1 of the Appendix. Assumption O5.2 uses the following quantities:

For (L3), the analogous candidate is series conditional quantile regression, with FQ​ a KQ,n​-dimensional series class, run on the treated observations that the estimated boundary window selects. This section presents the experimental designs, estimands, and supporting numerical results. The replication package gives the random seeds, learner tuning, numerical grids, solver options, and run instructions used to produce every exhibit.

J.1 Synthetic Experiment: Data-Generating Process

Continuous instrument. The DGP has the following components:
  • Instrument and latent resistance. Z∼Unif(0,1), independent of everything else, and U∼Unif(0,1).
  • Propensity score and treatment. The propensity score is p(Z)=logistic(β0​+β1​Z) with β0​=−1 and β1​=2, so p(Z) ranges from logistic(−1)≈0.27 to logistic(1)≈0.73. Treatment follows the threshold-crossing rule W=1(U⩽p(Z)).
  • Potential outcomes. With ε∼Unif(−0.5,0.5), define Y(1)=aU+θ+ε and Y(0)=aU+ε, where a=0.5 and θ=0.5. The common shock is therefore part of both potential outcomes, so consistency gives Y=WY(1)+(1−W)Y(0). Thus Y(0) ranges over [−0.5,1] and Y(1) over [0,1.5], so the tightest common bound is [ymin​,ymax​]=[−0.5,1.5], and both endpoints are attained.
The MTE is constant: MTE(u)=E[Y(1)−Y(0)∣U=u]=θ=0.5 for all u. The policy of interest is qα​(Z)=clip(p(Z)+α,0,1), and the target parameter is
θα​=E[Yqα​−Y]=θ⋅E[1(U⩽qα​(Z))−1(U⩽p(Z))].
Over the reported range ∣α∣⩽0.12 we have p(Z)+α∈[0.15,0.85]⊂[0,1], so clipping is inactive and E[1(U⩽qα​(Z))−1(U⩽p(Z))]=α. The ground truth is therefore exact:
θα​=θ⋅α=0.5α.
Discrete instrument. The DGP has the following components, with a propensity score that takes only two values:
  • Instrument and latent resistance. Z∼Bernoulli(0.5) (binary) and U∼Unif(0,1), independent of each other.
  • Propensity score and treatment. The propensity score is piecewise constant with two levels:
    p(Z)={0.250.75​if Z=0,if Z=1.​
    Treatment follows the threshold-crossing rule W=1(U⩽p(Z)).
  • Potential outcomes. Let ε∼Unif(−0.1,0.1) be independent of (U,Z) and define Y(0)=0.1+0.22U+ε and Y(1)=0.58+0.40U+ε. The common shock is therefore part of both potential outcomes, so consistency gives Y=WY(1)+(1−W)Y(0). The treatment effect remains τ(U)=Y(1)−Y(0)=0.48+0.18U, and hence MTE(u)=0.48+0.18u, ranging from 0.48 to 0.66. The resulting outcome support is contained in [ymin​,ymax​]=[0,1.08].
The target parameter is θα​=E[Yqα​−Y] under the same uniform policy shift qα​(Z)=clip(p(Z)+α,0,1). For the reported range ∣α∣⩽0.12, clipping is inactive at both propensity values. Thus the following ground truth is exact (with oriented integrals when α<0):
θα​=21​∫0.250.25+α​(0.48+0.18u)du+21​∫0.750.75+α​(0.48+0.18u)du=0.57α+0.09α2.

What is identified is the aggregate over the complier block: differencing the two instrument arms gives E[Y∣Z=1]−E[Y∣Z=0]=∫0.250.75​MTE(u)du, that is, the complier average LATE=0.51​∫0.250.75​MTE(u)du, together with the marginal laws of Y(1) and Y(0) for the block U∈(0.25,0.75] as a whole. The policy shift qα​ moves mass over the sub-block (0.25,0.25+α], which is strictly finer than the identified block, and over (0.75,0.75+α], on which nothing beyond the outcome support is known.
Discrete instrument with covariates. The DGP has the following components, with five covariates and a three-valued instrument:
  • Covariates and indices. X∼Unif(−1,1)5, and two scalar indices drive the design: ξ(X)=Λ(X′β1​) with β1​=(1.5,−1.2,0.9,−0.6,0.3) and Λ the logistic function, and ζ(X)=X′β2​ with β2​ the β1​-orthogonalized, unit-normalized version of (−0.6,0.9,1.2,0.3,−1.5). Sample sizes and comparison methods. The continuous and discrete instrument experiments both use n=5,000 observations, and the covariate design uses n=4,000 for the reported identified sets and n ranging from 1,000 to 16,000 for the Monte Carlo study. We approximate the unrestricted MTR with flexible u-spline sieves. In the covariate design, the sieve is interacted with all five covariates, and we report degrees 3 and 7. Degree 7 is the richest sieve that solves reliably across the policy grid without numerical error. The replication package provides the spline bases, the fitted propensity model, target-weight construction, solver settings, and bootstrap configuration.

3 reports the continuous-design bounds for different values of α>0, together with the IVMTE 95% backward confidence interval; the full grid is plotted in 2. On the single draw of 3 the truth falls inside the estimated IVOT interval at 24 of the 25 grid points, with the exception at α=0.01. The population IVOT interval has width of order α2 near zero: its width is 4×10−4 at ∣α∣=0.01 and 0.045 at ∣α∣=0.12. The estimated IVOT interval is 0.79–1.06 times as wide as the population sharp set and contains the truth at all 11 grid points. Its width is within 6% of the sharp width at nine points. At the two leftmost shifts, the estimated policy level merges with a neighboring baseline level because the design is close to the separation boundary, producing the narrower intervals marked in the table. The baseline level sets are recovered throughout.

Monte Carlo study. We draw 400 independent samples at each of n=1,000, 2,000, 4,000, 8,000 and 16,000, and apply the procedure of 1 at α=0.22, with the nuisance functions fitted by gradient-boosted trees. We report the W=1 component studied in Theorem 4.7; 7 collects the results.

J.3 Bed Net Application: Data and Setup

Dataset. We use data from Dupas (2014), which studies insecticide-treated bed net (ITN) take-up among Kenyan households. The instrument is the offered price Z taking 17 distinct values spanning 0–250 Kenyan shillings. The treatment W∈{0,1} indicates ITN purchase and the outcome Y∈{0,1} indicates ITN usage at a one-year follow-up. The estimation sample consists of n=1078 observations after merging the purchase and follow-up datasets. Follow-up usage was not collected for households that did not purchase a net; we set Y=0 for these households, since a household that acquired no net through the program cannot use a study net. Purchasers with a missing follow-up response are dropped. Coding non-purchasers as Y=0 makes the outcome use of a study net, so that Y(0)=0 holds by construction: a household that buys no net through the program has no study net to use, whatever it does about malaria protection otherwise. Dropping purchasers without a follow-up response requires follow-up to be missing at random among purchasers, conditional on the offered price:
P(R=1∣Y(1),Z,W=1)=P(R=1∣Z,W=1),
where R indicates an observed follow-up. The reported intervals condition on this assumption, which we do not test: attrition that varies with usage would differ across price arms, since purchase depends on the instrument.
Propensity score estimation. We estimate the propensity score by logistic regression of W on the offered price Z. The fitted propensity decreases from 0.854 at zero price to 0.232 at the reference price of 150 KSh. Relative to cell-by-cell estimation across the 17 price levels, the logistic fit smooths the first stage and imposes monotonicity through the fitted price coefficient. The replication package provides the fitted model and diagnostics.
Policy and target. Both policies compared here are fixed-price policies. The baseline policy assigns every household the reference price z0​=150 KSh, giving the constant propensity p^​(z0​)≈0.232; the alternative policy qα​ raises that constant to qα​=min(p^​(z0​)+α,1) for α∈[0.05,αmax​]. The target is accordingly
PRTEα​=αE[Yqα​−Yp(z0​)]​,
the average per-unit effect of raising the purchase probability by α above its level at the reference price. Because both policies are constant in Z, the mean policy shift E[qα​−p(z0​)] equals α exactly. The baseline here is the fixed-price policy p(z0​); the other experiments instead use the observed assignment p(Z).

J.4 Bed Net Application: Numerical Results

8 reports the IVOT and IVMTE bounds for PRTEα​ at selected subsidy levels, together with 95% confidence intervals for both methods, the IVMTE interval being paired with the degree-20 point bounds it was computed from. IVOT yields tighter bounds throughout, and its estimated lower bound is positive at every reported subsidy level. The IVOT 95% delta-method CI remains inconclusive for the three smallest reported shifts and rules out non-positive per-unit effects from α=0.211 onward. The IVMTE 95% backward CI is likewise inconclusive at small α. At large α (near the maximum feasible shift), the IVOT bounds nearly point-identify PRTEα​, whereas the IVMTE identified set and its 95% CI remain substantially wider. The near-point identification arrives in a periodic pattern: the bounds tighten to near-zero width and then widen slightly as additional complier groups enter the policy margin.
The narrow estimated IVOT identified sets do not translate one-for-one into narrower confidence intervals. IVOT relies on treated-outcome quantities estimated separately across the 17 price cells, several of which contain few purchasers, whereas IVMTE pools information through its moment restrictions and sieve; the resulting variability in the IVOT bounds remains substantial, and division by α magnifies it at small policy shifts.
